extracting-from-pdfs-html-docx.explain:
## What it is

RAG quality starts **before embeddings**. You must turn files into text the retriever can stand on. **PDF** is a page-layout format: glyphs on a canvas. Reading order, columns, tables, and headers must be reconstructed. Scanned PDFs have **no text** and need **OCR**. **HTML** has real structure (headings, lists, tables) but is polluted with nav, cookies, footers, and scripts — extract main content. **DOCX** is zipped XML with styles; headings and lists survive if you read style names instead of flattening.

A two-column PDF extracted line-by-line interleaves sentences that never existed. The embedding then represents nonsense. Always spot-check a sample of real documents and keep page, URL, and title as metadata.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, 'the model is dumb' is often bad extraction. Interviewers will ask why PDF is harder than DOCX. They want layout vs structured XML, and OCR for scans. They will ding 'we just parsed text'. Take-homes that skip a sample inspection look junior.

## How it works + one small example

Pick three real files: a two-column paper, a wiki HTML export, a styled DOCX. Run your extractor. Read the output. Example. The paper's abstract is intact; page 4 interleaves columns — you switch to a layout-aware tool. The wiki keeps the article and drops the sidebar. The DOCX keeps Heading 1.

Record extractor name and version on the document row so you can re-run when you change tools. Tables: if they flatten to gibberish, store an image or a CSV sidecar and mark `table=true`.

## Failure modes

1. **Naive PDF line order** on columns.

2. **HTML with nav repeated** in every chunk.

3. **Skipping OCR** on image-only PDFs and silently indexing empty pages.

4. **No sample inspection.** You trust the first ten files.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask to see a before/after on a two-column page. If they never opened the extracted text, the pipeline is untrusted. Ask how scans are detected.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- PDF is layout, not text; scans need OCR.
- HTML needs boilerplate removal; keep headings and lists.
- DOCX styles are structure — use them.
- Inspect real samples before you index the corpus.
- Store page, URL, title, extractor version.
- Tables often need a sidecar, not a flattened line.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Answers mix two unrelated topics from one page. What failed? A two-column PDF was read across columns. Use a layout-aware extractor, re-index, and verify those pages. The embedding cannot fix invented sentences. Then show the change you would ship the same week. What do you strip and keep from a company wiki HTML export? Strip nav, footers, cookies, scripts. Keep headings, lists, tables, code, and metadata (URL, title, modified). Headings drive later chunking and citations. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Why is PDF extraction harder than DOCX? PDF stores positioned glyphs for drawing. Reading order, columns, and tables are inferred. Scans have no text and need OCR. DOCX is XML with paragraph styles, so headings and lists are explicit. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I extract with a tool that matches the format: layout or OCR for PDFs, main-content for HTML, styles for DOCX. I inspect real samples and I keep page and source metadata.
keyPoints: PDF is layout, not text; scans need OCR.
HTML needs boilerplate removal; keep headings and lists.
DOCX styles are structure — use them.
Inspect real samples before you index the corpus.
Store page, URL, title, extractor version.
Tables often need a sidecar, not a flattened line.

cleaning-while-keeping-structure.explain:
## What it is

Cleaning is not `text.strip()`. You **normalise** whitespace, hyphenated line breaks, encoding, and repeated headers/footers, while **keeping structure** that chunking and citations need: headings, lists, tables, code blocks, and metadata (title, section path, page). If you flatten to a bag of words you lose the only signals that later let you chunk by section or cite a heading.

Useful structure belongs in **metadata** and in lightweight markup you will not embed as noise. A header repeated on every page should be stripped from the body and stored once as `doc_title`. A list should stay a list.

Cleaning is also where you drop secrets (keys, PAN-looking numbers) before they enter the index.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, over-cleaning deletes the H2 that would have made a perfect chunk boundary. Under-cleaning leaves 'Page 4 of 40' in every chunk and tanks embeddings. Interviewers will ask what you keep. They want headings and metadata, not a purity spiral.

## How it works + one small example

Write a cleaner with tests on fixtures: a page with a running header, a hyphenated `inter-
national`, a `<h2>`, a bullet list. Example. You lift `Acme Policy v3` into `doc_title`, join hyphenated breaks, keep `## 2. Refunds`, drop the page number from the body, store `page=12`.

Do not run a general 'summarise to clean' LLM over the corpus unless you have a loss metric. Deterministic rules you can test beat a silent rewrite.

## Failure modes

1. **Flatten everything.** Chunking later has no headings.

2. **Leaving running headers** in every page chunk.

3. **LLM-rewrite as cleaning** with no diff.

4. **Not stripping secrets** before index.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask what a heading looks like after clean. If it is gone, chunking will be blind. Ask for a fixture test on a running header.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Strip repeated headers/footers; keep headings and lists.
- Store title, section path, and page as metadata.
- Join hyphenated line breaks; normalise encoding.
- Do not flatten the document into a bag of words.
- Deterministic cleaners you can test beat silent LLM rewrites.
- Drop secrets before the text hits the index.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Every chunk starts with Policy v3 | Page N. What do you change? Detect the running header, store the title once, drop it from the body. Re-embed. The repeated prefix was poisoning similarity. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Why not ask a model to 'clean and rewrite' every document? It can drop clauses, invent sentences, and you cannot diff loss cheaply. Use tested rules first. If you must rewrite, measure deletion of must-keep spans. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What structure do you keep while cleaning, and why? Headings, lists, tables, code, and metadata (title, section, page). Chunking and citations need them. Repeated headers and page numbers are noise and go to metadata or the bin. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I clean noise — headers, hyphen breaks, boilerplate — and I keep headings, lists, and metadata. Structure is for chunking and citations, not decoration.
keyPoints: Strip repeated headers/footers; keep headings and lists.
Store title, section path, and page as metadata.
Join hyphenated line breaks; normalise encoding.
Do not flatten the document into a bag of words.
Deterministic cleaners you can test beat silent LLM rewrites.
Drop secrets before the text hits the index.

questions.a: Source URL or path, title, section path, page, language, extractor version, and last-modified if you have it. Chunking will inherit these.

duplicates-updates-re-indexing.explain:
## What it is

Corpora are not write-once. You will see **duplicate files** (the same policy emailed twice), **updates** (v3 replaces v2), and **deletes**. The index must **upsert by a stable document id**, not append forever. Duplicates waste retrieval slots and confuse citations. Stale versions answer yesterday's question with last year's rule.

Incremental re-index means: hash or version the source, re-extract only what changed, delete or **tombstone** removed ids, and rebuild ANN structures as the engine requires. A weekly full rebuild is acceptable for small corpora; at scale it is how you run stale for six days.

Identity is the design: `id = source_system + native_id` (or a canonical URL), not the file name the intern chose.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, 'why do we cite two slightly different refund policies?' is a duplicate/version bug. Interviewers will ask how you update a document. They want upsert, version, and delete — not 'we re-embed the folder'. They will ding an append-only index.

## How it works + one small example

Document row: `{doc_id, version, content_hash, source, updated_at}`. On ingest: if hash unchanged, skip; if id exists and hash changed, replace chunks for that id; if source says deleted, remove chunks and tombstone. Example. Policy URL `/refund` updates. You replace chunks for `doc:wiki:refund`, you do not add `refund (1).pdf` as a sibling.

Near-duplicates (same text, different URL): decide a canonical id or you will retrieve both. Simhash or exact-hash on normalised text helps.

## Failure modes

1. **Append-only.** v1 and v3 both retrieve.

2. **Id = file name.** `Policy (2).pdf` is a new doc forever.

3. **No delete path.** Removed pages still answer.

4. **Full rebuild only**, never incremental, so updates wait a week.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask what the doc_id is. If it is the file name, reject. Ask to see an update and a delete in the pipeline, not only an insert.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Stable doc id from the source system, not the file name.
- Upsert on change; skip unchanged hashes.
- Replace chunks for an id; do not append a sibling.
- Tombstone or delete removals.
- Near-duplicates need a canonical id.
- Incremental ingest for anything that is not tiny.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Users get two refund answers that disagree by a year. What is wrong? v1 was never removed or the id was the file name so v3 became a sibling. Upsert by canonical id and delete the old chunks. Then show the change you would ship the same week. What is a tombstone here? A delete marker so retrieval and incremental jobs know the id is gone, even if a replica or cache still holds vectors until compaction. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: How do you handle an updated document in a vector index? Detect change via hash or version, replace that doc_id's chunks, re-embed, and update the ANN structure as required. Do not append a second copy. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I upsert by a stable document id, I skip unchanged hashes, I replace chunks on update, and I tombstone deletes. Append-only indexes are how you cite last year's policy.
keyPoints: Stable doc id from the source system, not the file name.
Upsert on change; skip unchanged hashes.
Replace chunks for an id; do not append a sibling.
Tombstone or delete removals.
Near-duplicates need a canonical id.
Incremental ingest for anything that is not tiny.

questions.q: Why not use the file name as the document id?
questions.a: Names change (copy, download, Policy (2).pdf). Native ids or canonical URLs stay stable across updates.

ocr-vs-born-digital-text.explain:
## What it is

**Born-digital** PDFs contain a text layer: extraction can recover characters (still with layout issues). **Scanned** PDFs are pictures of pages: you need **OCR** (and often layout analysis). OCR **drops or mangles tables**, confuses columns, and introduces word errors. You will not get DOCX-like structure from a scan. Detect which kind you have (text layer density, or a flag from the scanner) and route accordingly.

Saying 'we extract PDFs' without this split is how empty pages enter the index. Measuring OCR quality on a labelled page (word error rate, table survival) is part of ingest, not a nice-to-have.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask when OCR is required. The answer is: when there is no usable text layer. On the job, mixed folders (half scans) are the default in enterprises. A single extractor for both is a silent quality hole.

## How it works + one small example

Heuristic: if extracted text length / page is below a threshold, OCR that page. Example. A 40-page policy: pages 1–30 born-digital, 31–40 are signed scans. You OCR 31–40, you mark `ocr=true`, you accept that the signature table is unreliable, and you may store the image for a human.

Do not OCR born-digital by default: you pay latency and you can add errors. Do not skip OCR on scans: you index nothing.

## Failure modes

1. **One path for all PDFs.**

2. **OCR on already-good text** (cost and new errors).

3. **Trusting OCR tables** as facts.

4. **No `ocr` flag** so you cannot explain a bad cite.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask how they detect scans. If the answer is we OCR everything, they are wasting money and adding errors. Ask what happens to tables.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- OCR is for pages without a usable text layer.
- Born-digital still needs layout reconstruction.
- OCR mangles tables; do not treat them as facts.
- Detect per page; mixed documents are common.
- Flag ocr=true on those chunks.
- Measure word error on a sample; do not assume.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Half the corpus retrieves as empty. What do you check? Whether those PDFs are scans with no text layer. Route them through OCR, flag them, and re-index. A born-digital extractor will silently yield nothing. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Why might you still not trust a number from an OCR'd table? OCR table reconstruction is weak. Prefer a human or a structured source for figures. You can store the page image next to the chunk. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: When is OCR required for a PDF? When the page has no usable text layer — a scan or an image. Born-digital pages should use the text layer plus layout, not OCR by default. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Scanned PDFs need OCR and will drop tables; born-digital keeps a text layer but still needs layout. I detect which I have and I mark OCR pages in metadata.
keyPoints: OCR is for pages without a usable text layer.
Born-digital still needs layout reconstruction.
OCR mangles tables; do not treat them as facts.
Detect per page; mixed documents are common.
Flag ocr=true on those chunks.
Measure word error on a sample; do not assume.

questions.a: No. You add cost and new errors. Use the text layer; reserve OCR for pages that need it.

preserving-headings-and-lists.explain:
## What it is

**Headings and lists** are the cheapest structure you will ever get. They tell chunking where a section starts and they tell citations what to show ('§2 Refunds'). If you flatten them, recursive splitters have nothing to respect and users see a wall of text. Keep heading text and level in metadata (`section_path: Policy > Refunds > Exceptions`) and keep list items as lines under that heading.

This is why you paid for a decent extractor. Throwing the structure away in the next function is a common own-goal.

Code blocks and tables are the siblings: do not split a list item from its heading if you can keep them in one parent.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask how chunking knows about sections. The answer starts here, in ingest. On the job, a corpus with `section_path` is a joy; a flattened corpus is a year of 'why is this chunk mid-sentence'.

## How it works + one small example

After extract, a tree: `H1 / H2 / p / ul`. Serialise as markdown-ish text plus metadata. Example. `## 2. Refunds` stays, bullets stay, `section_path=['Refunds']` on those chunks. A later structural chunker splits on H2.

Test: a fixture with two H2s must produce two section_paths, not one blob. If the extractor lost styles, fix extract — do not invent headings with an LLM unless you measure.

## Failure modes

1. **`.get_text()`** that drops tags.

2. **Headings only in the first chunk** of a long section, children have none.

3. **Invented headings** that do not exist in the source.

4. **Lists joined into a paragraph** so items become one sentence.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask to see section_path on a middle chunk. If only the first chunk of a section has the heading, the metadata is wrong. Ask what flattened get_text would have destroyed.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Headings and lists are chunking and citation signals.
- Store section_path on every chunk in the section.
- Do not flatten tags in the first convenience function.
- Keep list items as items under their heading.
- Fix lost styles at extract time, not with guessed headings.
- Propagate the heading to child chunks, not only the first.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Long-section child chunks have no heading. What did you forget? To copy section_path (and maybe a heading prefix) onto every chunk in the section, not only the first. Retrieval of a middle chunk otherwise has no title. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you serialise a heading-plus-list for later chunking? Keep a markdown-like heading, keep bullets as lines, and set section_path metadata. A structural splitter can then cut on the heading. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Why preserve headings and lists through ingest? So chunking can split on sections and citations can show a heading. Flattened text loses the only cheap structure most corpora have. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I keep headings and lists in the body and in section_path metadata so chunking can respect sections and citations can name them. Flattening is how I throw away ingest work.
keyPoints: Headings and lists are chunking and citation signals.
Store section_path on every chunk in the section.
Do not flatten tags in the first convenience function.
Keep list items as items under their heading.
Fix lost styles at extract time, not with guessed headings.
Propagate the heading to child chunks, not only the first.

incremental-ingest-and-deletes.explain:
## What it is

**Incremental ingest** re-processes **changed** documents only. **Deletes** remove or tombstone their chunks so they cannot retrieve. Together they keep the index **fresh** without a nightly full rebuild. You need a change feed or a crawl with `updated_at`/`content_hash`, a queue, and an idempotent worker that upserts by `doc_id`.

Deletes are the part teams skip. A page taken down for legal reasons that still answers in the bot is an incident. Tombstones also stop a replica from resurrecting a vector after a partial deploy.

Measure freshness: p95 time from source change to searchable. That is an ingest SLO, not an embedding footnote.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask how you re-index. They want incremental + delete, not 'we drop and rebuild'. On the job, rebuild-only is why policy changes take a week and why legal deletes fail.

## How it works + one small example

Worker: pull change `{id, op: upsert|delete, hash}`. Upsert: extract/clean/chunk/embed/swap chunks in a transaction-like sequence (write new, flip pointer, delete old). Delete: remove vectors and mark tombstone.

Example. Legal unpublishes `/old-promo`. Within the SLO, that id is gone from search. A full rebuild on Sunday is a backstop, not the path.

If the engine cannot delete cheaply, schedule compaction and hide tombstoned ids at query time.

## Failure modes

1. **No delete.** Legal still retrieves.

2. **Rebuild as the only path.** Freshness is a week.

3. **Non-idempotent workers** that double-insert on retry.

4. **Flip pointer before new chunks exist.** A gap where the doc vanishes then reappears.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask for the delete path and the freshness SLO. If ingest is insert-only plus a Sunday rebuild, legal deletes fail. Ask how a retry does not duplicate.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Incremental: hash or updated_at, upsert by doc_id.
- Deletes are first-class; tombstone if the engine is slow to compact.
- Idempotent workers; retries must not duplicate.
- Write new chunks, then flip, then drop old — avoid a gap.
- Measure time from source change to searchable.
- Full rebuild is a backstop.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Legal unpublished a page; the bot still cites it. What is missing? A delete path. Add tombstone/remove on unpublish, hide those ids at query, and measure the SLO. Do not wait for Sunday's rebuild. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you avoid a gap during an update? Write the new chunks, atomically point the doc at them, then delete the old ones. Do not delete first. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What does incremental ingest do that a full rebuild does not? It processes only changed ids so freshness is hours or minutes, not a week. It still needs a delete/tombstone path for removals. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I re-index only changed documents and I tombstone removals. Freshness is an SLO. A weekly rebuild is a backstop, not the delete path.

Deletes are first-class; tombstone if the engine is slow to compact.
Idempotent workers; retries must not duplicate.
Write new chunks, then flip, then drop old — avoid a gap.
Measure time from source change to searchable.
Full rebuild is a backstop.

questions.a: p95 time from source change (or delete) to the id being searchable or gone. That is the ingest SLO.

interview.explain:
## What it is

**Interview: ingest a messy PDF corpus** is a spoken pipeline: **extract** (layout/OCR), **clean** (keep headings, drop headers), **dedupe/upsert**, and **measure loss** (sample pages, empty-page rate, table survival, freshness). You name metadata (page, section_path, ocr flag, doc_id). You do not start at embeddings.

This is M4.1's exam. They want the pipeline and the metrics, not a library name.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

It is a common opener for RAG interviews because most corpora are PDFs. Candidates who jump to chunk size have not ingested. On the job this is also the first-week plan for a new corpus.

## How it works + one small example

Say, in order:

1. Sample the folder: born-digital vs scan, columns, tables.
2. Extract with the matching tool; inspect pages.
3. Clean: headers out, headings in, secrets out.
4. Id = canonical URL or native id; upsert; delete path.
5. Measure: empty pages, OCR word error, duplicate rate, time-to-searchable.

Close: 'I would not embed until I have read twenty extracted pages.'

## Failure modes

1. **Starting at chunk size.**

2. **No OCR mention** on a scan-heavy corpus.

3. **No loss metric.**

4. **File name as id.**


## How you would defend it in a review

Time the pipeline speech. If embeddings appear before extract/clean/id, they fail the talking point. Ask how they would measure loss on Monday.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Speak extract → clean → upsert → measure, not embed first.
- Split OCR vs born-digital in the first minute.
- Name doc_id, section_path, and a delete path.
- Loss metrics: empty pages, OCR error, duplicates, freshness.
- Read extracted pages before you index.
- File name is not an id.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A candidate starts with chunk size 512. What did they skip? Whether the text exists and is in reading order. Chunking garbage yields garbage. Inspect extraction first. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Which loss numbers do you quote? Empty-page rate, OCR word error on a labelled page, duplicate rate, table survival if you need tables, and p95 time from change to searchable. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Extract with layout or OCR as needed, clean while keeping headings, upsert/dedupe by a stable id with a delete path, and measure loss on samples (empty pages, OCR error, duplicates, freshness). Then, and only then, chunk and embed. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** What identifiers and flags do you mention?

Canonical doc_id, section_path, page, ocr=true when applicable, extractor version. Not the file name.

**recall.** What one sentence closes the answer?

I would not embed until I have read a sample of extracted pages and I can upsert and delete.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

Extract, clean, dedupe, measure loss. I inspect real pages, I upsert by a stable id, and I do not talk about embeddings until the text is trustworthy.

why-documents-must-be-split.explain:
## What it is

Embedding models and context windows have **limits**. A 80-page policy cannot be one vector and cannot be one prompt. **Chunking** splits text into pieces you embed and retrieve. The piece must be small enough to embed well and to fit several of them in the generator's window, and large enough to be understandable without its siblings.

You split because **retrieval is nearest-neighbour on chunks**, not on documents. A document-level vector averages away the refund paragraph you needed. You also split because updates and citations are chunk-grained: you replace and cite a span, not a book.

Splitting is a product decision (what the user will see) as well as a model-limit decision.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask why we chunk. They want limits plus retrieval granularity, not 'because the tutorial did'. On the job, refusing to split (one vector per PDF) is how you retrieve the wrong chapter.

## How it works + one small example

Show the numbers. Model useful length ~8k tokens; you want 3–8 chunks in the prompt; each chunk 200–800 tokens is a common starting band. A 40k-token manual becomes ~80 chunks, not 1. Example. Query 'late fee'. A doc-level vector ranks a whole credit-card agreement; a chunk-level vector ranks the late-fee section.

Keep the parent doc_id so you can expand context later (parent-child).

## Failure modes

1. **One vector per PDF.**

2. **Chunks larger than the window** so one result fills the prompt.

3. **Chunks so small** they are single sentences with no meaning.

4. **Forgetting parent id** so you cannot expand.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask why they chunk. If they only say the model has a limit, add retrieval granularity. Ask what happens with one vector per PDF.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Windows and embedders have length limits.
- Retrieval is over chunks, not whole documents.
- A doc-level vector averages away the paragraph you need.
- Chunk size must leave room for several hits in the prompt.
- Keep parent doc_id for expansion and citations.
- Splitting is a product choice, not only a model limit.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. You embedded each PDF as one vector and late-fee questions miss. Why? The late-fee paragraph was averaged with 40 pages of other terms. Chunk so that section is its own vector, and keep the parent id. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do window limits affect chunk size? You need several chunks in the generator prompt. If one chunk is the whole window, you cannot add neighbours or a question. Start from a band that leaves room for k>1. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Why must documents usually be split before embedding? Embedders and prompts have length limits, and retrieval is nearest-neighbour on the unit you embed. A whole-document vector averages mixed topics and cannot fit beside other evidence. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I split so retrieval can find a span the embedder can represent and the generator can afford. Documents are too big and too mixed to be one vector.

Keep parent doc_id for expansion and citations.
Splitting is a product choice, not only a model limit.

fixed-recursive-structural-semantic.explain:
## What it is

Four families you should be able to name. **Fixed-size**: every N tokens, simple, ignores meaning. **Recursive**: split on headings, then paragraphs, then sentences, then tokens until under a cap — the usual default. **Structural**: use the document tree (H2, table, function) as the unit. **Semantic**: split where topic similarity drops. Real systems mix: structural or recursive first, semantic only if an eval says so.

Fixed is a baseline. Recursive is the workhorse. Structural wins on manuals and code. Semantic is costlier and can drift. Do not start with semantic because it sounds smart.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask you to compare chunkers. They want this list and a default (recursive/structural). On the job, picking semantic first is how you spend a week for a 1-point lift.

## How it works + one small example

Start recursive with heading separators. Example. Policy markdown: split on `##`, then `###`, then paragraphs to stay under 600 tokens. Code: split on function boundaries (structural). A novel: fixed or recursive on paragraphs. Semantic: only after recall@k is measured and you have a reason boundaries are wrong.

Keep the same metadata regardless of family.

## Failure modes

1. **Semantic first** with no baseline.

2. **Fixed-size through tables and functions.**

3. **Recursive with no heading separators** (it is just fixed).

4. **A different family per file type** with no note in the pipeline.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask them to name four families. If they only know fixed, they are not ready. Ask which they ship first and why.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Fixed, recursive, structural, semantic — know all four.
- Recursive/structural is the usual default.
- Fixed is a baseline, not a destination for structured docs.
- Semantic is extra cost; measure first.
- Match family to file type (code ≠ prose).
- Metadata stays the same across families.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A teammate starts with semantic chunking on day one. What do you do? Ship recursive/structural, measure recall, then try semantic as an A/B. Semantic first is unearned cost and a harder pipeline. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you chunk a markdown policy versus a source file? Policy: recursive on headings then paragraphs. Source: structural on functions or classes so you do not split a function mid-body. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Name four chunking families and the usual default. Fixed-size, recursive, structural, and semantic. Default is recursive (or structural when you have a tree). Fixed is a baseline. Semantic is later and measured. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I can name fixed, recursive, structural, and semantic. I start recursive or structural, I treat fixed as a baseline, and I add semantic only if an eval asks for it.

size-overlap-boundaries-metadata.explain:
## What it is

Four knobs. **Size**: tokens (or characters) per chunk — trade precision vs context. **Overlap**: repeated tail/head so a sentence that sat on a boundary still appears whole. **Boundaries**: prefer heading/paragraph/sentence ends; do not cut mid-table or mid-function. **Metadata**: inherit doc_id, section, page; you will filter and cite with it.

These knobs affect **retrieval quality** more than people expect. Too big: mixed topics, one hit fills the window. Too small: no meaning, you retrieve a clause without the exception. Overlap too high: near-duplicate hits waste k. Overlap zero: boundary sentences vanish.

Start from the embedder's useful length, not from a blog's 512.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the most-asked chunking interview. They want the four knobs and how each hurts. On the job, these are the first A/Bs after ingest works.

## How it works + one small example

Pick a starting band (e.g. 400–800 tokens, 10–15% overlap, split on headings). Example. 800 tokens, 80 overlap, markdown headers. Eval recall@5. If questions need a heading plus a far exception, grow size or add parent-child. If k is full of twins, drop overlap or diversify.

Never tune size without an eval set. 'It looks nicer' is not a knob change.

## Failure modes

1. **Size from a tweet**, not the embedder.

2. **50% overlap** and k full of dupes.

3. **Cut mid-table** because the counter said 512.

4. **Metadata dropped** at split time.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask for the four knobs and one failure each. If they only say 512, they have not designed. Ask how metadata is copied.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Size, overlap, boundaries, metadata — four knobs.
- Start from embedder length and prompt budget.
- Overlap saves boundary sentences; too much wastes k.
- Respect tables, functions, and headings.
- Inherit metadata onto every child chunk.
- Tune with recall, not vibes.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. k=5 is three near-copies of the same paragraph. What knob do you touch? Overlap is probably high, or the splitter is emitting sliding windows. Reduce overlap and/or add diversity. Do not just raise k. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you pick a starting size? From the embedder's useful length and how many chunks you want in the generator window (k times size plus question). Then measure recall and adjust. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What four chunking knobs do you name, and what does each risk? Size (too big mixes topics; too small lacks meaning), overlap (too much duplicates; too little drops boundary sentences), boundaries (mid-table/function cuts), metadata (lost cites and filters). Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I set size from the embedder and the prompt budget, I overlap just enough to save boundary sentences, I split on real boundaries, and I inherit metadata. I change knobs only against recall.

precise-chunks-vs-context-rich-chunks.explain:
## What it is

**Small precise chunks** retrieve the right sentence and starve the generator of surrounding rules. **Large context-rich chunks** give the generator enough to answer and retrieve mixed or off-topic text. This is a **trade-off**, not a virtue contest. The usual synthesis is **small to retrieve, large to generate**: parent-child or small-to-big (next note).

If you can only have one size, pick from the failure you have. Missing the clause → smaller. Answers that ignore an exception two paragraphs away → larger or parent expansion.

Do not grow chunks to hide a bad embedder. Measure both retrieval hit rate and answer faithfulness.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will force a pick. The senior move is to name the trade-off and the two-level pattern. On the job, this is the conversation you have after the first eval.

## How it works + one small example

Eval two sizes on the same questions. Example. 200-token chunks: high retrieval precision, answers miss the exception. 1200-token: retrieval noisier, answers complete. You keep 200 for search and send the 1200 parent to the model (parent-child). If you cannot implement two-level yet, pick 500–700 as a compromise and log the misses.

## Failure modes

1. **Always tiny** because 'precision'.

2. **Always huge** because 'context'.

3. **No eval**, only taste.

4. **Growing size to paper over a bad query.**


## How you would defend it in a review

Hear the trade-off and the two-level escape. If they pick a religion (always 128 or always 2048), push for the failure-driven pick.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Precision vs context is a trade-off.
- Retrieve small, generate large is the usual synthesis.
- Pick the single size from the failure you have.
- Measure hit rate and faithfulness, not only one.
- Do not grow chunks to hide a bad embedder or query.
- Parent-child is how you stop choosing only one.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Retrieval is accurate but answers miss a nearby exception. What do you change? Expand to the parent section at generate time, or grow the chunk slightly. Do not only raise k with more tiny twins. Then show the change you would ship the same week. When would you keep a single medium size? When you cannot ship two-level yet and an eval shows 500–700 tokens is good enough on both hit rate and faithfulness. Log the misses for a later parent-child. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What is the trade-off between small and large chunks? Small chunks retrieve the right span but starve the generator of nearby exceptions. Large chunks feed context but mix topics and waste the window. Name both, then prefer two-level if you can. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Small chunks retrieve; large chunks explain. I name the trade-off and I prefer retrieve-small, generate-large when I can. One size is a compromise I measure.

parent-child-and-small-to-big.explain:
## What it is

**Parent-child** (small-to-big) stores a **small child** you retrieve and a **larger parent** you send to the generator. The child is a paragraph or a heading-sized span; the parent is the section or a window around it. You get precise retrieval and context-rich generation without stuffing the index with huge vectors that mix topics.

Implementation: two ids, `parent_id` on the child, a lookup at query time after top-k children (dedupe parents). Do not send eight children that all expand to the same parent — you waste the window.

This is the standard answer to the previous trade-off.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers treat parent-child as a seniority tell. On the job it is the first serious chunking upgrade after recursive split. It also makes citations nicer (cite the child span, show the parent).

## How it works + one small example

Index children (~200–400 tokens). Store parents (~800–1500 or the H2 section). Query: embed the question, retrieve 8 children, map to unique parents (cap 3–4), send those. Example. Child hits the late-fee sentence; parent is §4 Fees. The model sees the exception two paragraphs down.

Dedup is mandatory. Eight children in one section become one parent.

## Failure modes

1. **No dedup.** Window is one section eight times.

2. **Parent too big** (the whole PDF).

3. **Child too big** (you lost precision).

4. **Citing the parent** when the span was the child — or the reverse without a quote.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask for the two ids and the dedup. If they embed only large chunks, they missed the pattern. Ask what they cite.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Retrieve children; generate with parents.
- Dedupe children that share a parent.
- Parent is a section or window, not the whole doc.
- Cite the child span; the parent is context.
- This is the standard fix for the precision/context trade-off.
- Cap how many unique parents you send.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Eight retrieved children expand to the same H2. What do you do? Dedupe on parent_id and send that parent once. Otherwise the window is wasted on copies. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How large should the parent be? The section or a modest window that contains the exception the child missed — not the entire document. If the parent is the PDF, you are back to doc-level context. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What is parent-child (small-to-big) chunking? Index and retrieve a small child span; at generate time send its larger parent section. You get precise retrieval and enough context without embedding huge mixed vectors. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I retrieve a small child and send its parent for context. I dedupe parents so k does not collapse to one section, and I cite the span I actually used.

table-and-code-block-boundaries.explain:
## What it is

**Never split a table row or a function mid-chunk** if you can avoid it. A half-row is not a fact; a half-function is not callable context. Treat tables, code blocks, and sometimes lists as **atomic units**: keep them together, even if you bust the size cap a bit, or store them as **sibling objects** (a CSV/json sidecar) with a pointer from the surrounding prose.

If a table is huge, split on **row groups** with the header repeated, not on a character count through a cell. If a function is huge, split on inner helpers, not mid-statement.

This is the boundary knob with teeth.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

On the job, RAG that quotes half a pricing table is how you ship a wrong price. Interviewers will ask how you chunk tables and code. They want atomic units, not 512. This is a favourite follow-up after size/overlap.

## How it works + one small example

Detector: markdown tables, HTML table elements, fenced code, `def `/`function `. Example. A 30-row fee table: one chunk with the header plus rows, or three chunks each with the **same header** + 10 rows. A 400-line file: one chunk per exported function.

If the embedder hates huge tables, embed a caption plus first rows and store the full table for generate-time fetch by id.

## Failure modes

1. **512 through a table.**

2. **Function split mid-if.**

3. **Dropping tables** because they were 'ugly'.

4. **Splitting rows without repeating the header.**


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask what happens at token 512 inside a table. If they cut, reject. Ask how a function is split. Ask whether numbers have a sidecar.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Do not split table rows or functions mid-unit.
- Bust the size cap a little or store a sidecar.
- Paginate tables by row groups with the header repeated.
- Code splits on function/class, not on token count alone.
- Huge tables can be fetched by id at generate time.
- Dropping tables silently is a product bug if users ask about numbers.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A retrieved chunk is the second half of a function and the model invents the signature. What failed? A token splitter cut the function. ## What it is

**Interview: pick a chunk size** is a method, not a number. **Start from the embedding model's useful length**, **measure recall**, then **adjust overlap** and boundaries. Mention parent-child if the trade-off appears. You do not say '512 because LangChain default'.

This is M4.2's exam. They want a starting band, an eval, and the next knob, in that order.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Every RAG interview asks this. Candidates who quote a default fail. Candidates who name embedder length, k, overlap, and recall pass. On the job this is also how you stop a bike-shed.

## How it works + one small example

Say:

1. 'Useful embedder length and how many chunks I want in the prompt give a starting band (e.g. 400–800).'
2. 'Recursive/structural split, small overlap, keep tables/functions intact.'
3. 'Measure recall@k on a labelled set; then move size or overlap, or add parent-child.'
4. 'I would not pick a number without that loop.'

Close: 'Start from the embedder, measure recall, then adjust overlap.'

## Failure modes

1. **A single number with no method.**

2. **Forgetting overlap and boundaries.**

3. **No eval.**

4. **Ignoring the generator window** (k × size).

what-an-embedding-represents.explain:
## What it is

An **embedding** is a **vector** that places a piece of text in a high-dimensional space so that **semantically related** pieces sit nearer than unrelated ones. 'Refund window' and 'how long to get my money back' should be closer than 'refund window' and 'office window hours'. The model that produces the vector was trained (contrastive or similar) so that a **distance or similarity** (usually cosine) approximates relatedness.

It is not a keyword index. It is not a knowledge store. It does not 'understand' in a legal sense. It is a geometric proxy you will retrieve with. Different models define different spaces; a number in one space is meaningless in another (later note).

The unit you embed (chunk, query, title) is the unit you will retrieve.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask what an embedding is. They want geometry plus a caveat, not 'magic meaning numbers'. On the job, this sentence stops people from treating cosine as truth.

## How it works + one small example

Show three sentences, two paraphrases and one pun. A decent embedder ranks the paraphrase above the pun. Example. Query 'close my account'. Near: 'how to terminate membership'. Far: 'bank account numbers format'. If your model ranks the pun first, the space is wrong for the job — or the chunk is.

Do not explain training maths unless asked. Explain the use: embed chunks at ingest, embed the query at ask, rank by similarity.

## Failure modes

1. **Calling it a knowledge base.** It cannot cite a fact it was not given.

2. **Treating cosine 0.82 as proof.**

3. **Embedding whole books** as one point.

4. **Mixing models** (next notes).


## How you would defend it in a review

Hear geometry plus caveat. If they say the embedding knows the answer, correct them. Ask what unit they embed.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Embeddings are vectors; nearby ≈ related in that model's space.
- They are not keyword indexes or knowledge bases.
- The embedded unit is the retrieved unit.
- Cosine is a proxy, not proof.
- Spaces are model-specific.
- Paraphrases should beat puns on a smoke test.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Cosine 0.9 between a query and a chunk. Are they the same fact? Not necessarily. They are nearby in that space. The chunk can still be outdated, off-entity, or a pun. You still cite and check. Then show the change you would ship the same week. What unit should you embed for RAG? The chunk you will retrieve (and maybe a title or query prefix). Embedding a whole book averages topics and cannot retrieve a paragraph. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What does a text embedding represent? A vector in a model-specific space where semantically related texts tend to lie nearer than unrelated ones. It is a retrieval proxy, not a knowledge store or a proof of truth. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

An embedding is a vector that puts related text nearby in one model's space. I use it as a retrieval proxy, not as a knowledge store or a proof.

They are not keyword indexes or knowledge bases.
The embedded unit is the retrieved unit.
Cosine is a proxy, not proof.
Spaces are model-specific.
Paraphrases should beat puns on a smoke test.

generating-embeddings.explain:
## What it is

You **generate** embeddings by sending text to an **embedding model** (API or local) and storing the returned vector with the chunk id. **Documents** are embedded at ingest (batch, offline). **Queries** are embedded at ask time (online, small). Use the **same model and version** for both, with any required **prefix** (next notes). Persist the vector, the model id, and the dim.

Batch the ingest side. Cap payload sizes. Retry 429s with a bound. Do not embed in a request path that the user is waiting on except for the query vector.

Never log the raw text next to the vector unless policy allows; the vector can still leak information, but the text is the obvious PII.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the mechanical skill. Interviewers want: same model for query and doc, batch ingest, store model id. On the job, embedding with two models is the classic silent recall crash.

## How it works + one small example

Ingest job: chunks → batch embed → write `{chunk_id, vector, model, dim}`. Query: one embed, search. Example. 50k chunks, 100 per batch, semaphore 4, store `text-embedding-3-large` and 3072. A later switch of model is a full re-embed, not a config flip.

Pin the snapshot. An alias that changes under you mixes spaces.

## Failure modes

1. **Different models** for query and doc.

2. **Not storing model id.** You cannot re-embed.

3. **Live-embedding the corpus** on each ask.

4. **Unbounded batch** that 429s the key.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask which model embeds the query. If it can drift from the corpus, reject. Ask where the model id is stored.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Same model and version for queries and documents.
- Batch ingest; embed the query online.
- Store vector, model id, and dimension.
- A model change is a full re-embed.
- Bound the ingest job like any other LLM/API call.
- Pin the snapshot; aliases mix spaces.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Recall collapsed after a 'model upgrade'. What happened? Query and docs are in different spaces, or only one side was re-embedded. Re-embed the corpus with the new id or roll back the query model. Then show the change you would ship the same week. What do you persist next to each vector? chunk_id, model id, dimension, and the text pointer. Without the model id you cannot know if a later query is in the same space. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: When do you embed documents versus queries? Documents at ingest, in bounded batches, stored with the vector. Queries at ask time, one vector per search. Both must use the same pinned model. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I embed documents at ingest in bounded batches and the query at ask time, with the same pinned model, and I store the model id and dim next to the vector.

choosing-an-embedding-model.explain:
## What it is

You choose on **quality for your language and domain**, **dimensions** (storage and ANN), **cost**, **latency**, and **licence**. Multilingual corpora need a multilingual model. Legal or medical jargon may want a domain model or a larger general one with good evals. Higher dimensions are not automatically better; they cost RAM and can hurt some ANN settings. Latency matters for the query embed (user is waiting). Cost matters for ingest of millions of chunks.

Do not pick from a leaderboard alone. Run **your** 50–200 queries. A 1-point MTEB win can lose on your tickets.

Open vs API is the Level 11 path question applied to embedders: data boundary vs convenience.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask how you pick. They want eval-on-your-data plus the practical axes, not a brand. On the job, swapping embedders is a re-index — so pick with a reason.

## How it works + one small example

Shortlist two models. Embed a labelled mini-corpus. Compare recall@k, p95 query embed latency, storage (n × dim × 4 bytes), and price. Example. API large vs local small: large wins 4 recall points, adds 80ms and a data-boundary review. You pick from the constraint, not the leaderboard.

Revisit when the corpus language or the SLA changes.

## Failure modes

1. **Leaderboard only.**

2. **Biggest dim** as a proxy for quality.

3. **Ignoring query latency.**

4. **Picking a monolingual model** for a two-language corpus.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask for their last eval, not a leaderboard. Ask dim, language, and whether a swap was priced as a re-index.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Eval on your queries, not only MTEB.
- Axes: quality, dim/storage, cost, latency, licence, language.
- Higher dim is not automatically better.
- Query embed is on the user path.
- A swap means re-embedding the corpus.
- Monolingual models fail mixed-language corpora.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A larger-dim model wins MTEB but loses on your tickets. Which do you ship? The one that wins on your tickets, unless a constraint (on-prem, cost) forbids it. Leaderboards are a shortlist, not a decision. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Why does query latency matter more than ingest latency? The user is waiting on the query embed plus search. Ingest is a batch job. A 300ms embedder can dominate p95. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What axes do you use to choose an embedding model? Quality on your labelled queries, language/domain fit, dimensions and storage, query latency, ingest cost, and licence/data boundary. Not a leaderboard alone. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I pick an embedder from my eval, language, dim/storage, cost, and latency — not from a leaderboard screenshot. A swap is a re-index, so I write the reason.

vector-spaces-cannot-be-mixed.explain:
## What it is

Vectors from **different models** live in **different spaces**. Dimensions may even match by accident; the axes still mean different things. **Cosine across models is meaningless.** You cannot store model A's chunks and query with model B. You cannot average them. You cannot build one ANN from mixed rows.

If you change model, **re-embed everything** and rebuild the index. If you must run two models (migration), you run **two indexes** and you never join scores across them without a calibrated fusion you have measured.

This is the interview line: 'why you cannot mix spaces'.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

The classic production bug: someone 'upgrades' the query embedder. Recall dies. Interviewers will ask why. They want this sentence. On the job, store the model id so the bug is visible.

## How it works + one small example

Guard: the query path reads `index.model_id` and embeds with that id, or it refuses. Example. Nightly job writes `3-large` vectors; a new service embeds queries with `minilm`. Scores are noise. You fail the query or you dual-run.

Migration: build index B, dual-query, compare, flip, delete A. Do not write B's vectors into A's table.

## Failure modes

1. **Query model ≠ index model.**

2. **Concatenating 1536 and 384** with padding.

3. **One table, two models**, no column.

4. **Averaging scores** from two spaces.


## How you would defend it in a review

Hear 'meaningless cosine'. If they think dim match is enough, fail. Ask how the query path knows the model id.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- One model per index; query and docs match.
- Equal dimension does not mean the same space.
- A model change is a full re-embed and rebuild.
- Two models means two indexes, not mixed rows.
- Store model_id and refuse a mismatch.
- This is a favourite interview line.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Recall died after a query-model upgrade. The dim is the same. What is wrong? Same dim, different space. Point the query at the old model or re-embed the corpus. Do not 'tune k'. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you migrate embedders without an outage? Build a second index, dual-query, compare recall, flip traffic, then delete the old index. Never write both models into one table. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Why can you not mix embeddings from two models? They define different vector spaces. Cosine (or L2) between them is not a semantic score, even if the dimensions match. Re-embed or run separate indexes. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Different embedders rotate the space. Cosine across models is meaningless. I pin one model per index and I re-embed the corpus when I change it.

instruction-tuned-vs-raw-embedding-model.explain:
## What it is

Some embedders are **instruction-tuned** or **asymmetric**: they expect a **query prefix** (`query: ...`) and a **document prefix** (`passage: ...`), or only a query instruction. Using the same raw string on both sides, or swapping prefixes, **tanks recall**. Raw / symmetric models (older sentence-transformers style) want the same treatment on both sides.

Read the model card. If it says 'use `query:` for searches', that is not decoration. Store the prefix policy next to the model id. Apply it in one function so ingest and query cannot drift.

HyDE and query rewrite still need the correct prefix on the **text you actually embed**.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is a silent killer after a model swap to e5/BGE/GTE-style models. Interviewers who have shipped these will ask. On the job, a missing `query:` is a 10-point recall hole that looks like a chunking bug.

## How it works + one small example

`embed(text, role)` adds the prefix from a table `{model, query_prefix, doc_prefix}`. Example. e5: docs `passage: {chunk}`, queries `query: {q}`. A teammate embeds both raw; recall drops; you diff the function and restore prefixes.

Test: a fixture asserts the exact bytes sent to the model for a query vs a doc.

## Failure modes

1. **Ignoring the card.**

2. **Prefix on docs only** or queries only.

3. **Two copies** of the prefix string that drift.

4. **Applying a query prefix to passages.**


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask what bytes go to the embedder for a query. If they never mention a prefix on a model that needs one, they will ship a recall hole. Ask for the test.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Some models need query vs passage prefixes.
- Mismatch looks like a chunking bug and is not.
- One function applies the policy for ingest and query.
- Read the model card; store the policy.
- Symmetric models want the same treatment both sides.
- Assert the bytes in a test.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. You switched to e5 and recall fell 12 points. Chunks are unchanged. What do you check? Query and passage prefixes. If both sides are raw, or swapped, restore the card's prefixes. Do not retune chunk size first. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you keep prefixes from drifting? A single embed(text, role) that reads policy from the model id, plus a test on the exact bytes. No second copy in the query service. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What is an instruction-tuned or asymmetric embedder? A model that expects different prefixes or instructions for queries versus documents. Using raw text on both sides, or the wrong prefix, collapses recall. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Instruction-tuned embedders expect a query prefix; mismatch tanks recall. I store the policy with the model id and I apply it in one function.

questions.a: You embed the hypothetical document (or the rewrite) with the **document** or **query** prefix the card says for that role — the role of the string you embed, not the user's original sentence.

dimensionality-and-storage-cost.explain:
## What it is

**Dimension** is the length of the vector. **Storage** is roughly `n_vectors × dim × bytes_per_value` plus ANN overhead (HNSW graphs can be several times the raw vectors). Higher dim can help quality and always costs **RAM**, disk, and often **latency**. It is **not automatic quality**. A 3072-d model that wins 0.5 recall points and costs 4× RAM may lose on a laptop-sized box or a small pgvector node.

Quantisation (int8, binary) trades quality for RAM. Matryoshka / shorter prefixes trade quality for dim. Measure both.

Plan capacity before you pick 'the biggest embedder'.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask why you did not pick the largest dim. They want this cost model. On the job, RAM is why teams stay on 384–768 or quantise.

## How it works + one small example

Compute: 5e6 chunks × 1536 × 4 bytes ≈ 30 GB raw, plus HNSW (often 2–3×). Example. You cannot fit that on a 16 GB app box. You pick 768-d, or quantise, or a dedicated store. A 0.8-point recall win is not worth an OOM.

Re-eval after quantisation; do not assume the card's quality holds on your queries.

## Failure modes

1. **Biggest dim** as default.

2. **Forgetting ANN overhead.**

3. **Quantising without an eval.**

4. **n × dim in a spreadsheet that ignores replicas.**


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask them to compute n × dim for their corpus. If they never mention ANN overhead, the estimate is low. Ask whether the biggest dim was a default.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Storage ≈ n × dim × bytes plus ANN overhead.
- Higher dim ≠ automatic quality.
- Query latency and RAM matter as much as MTEB.
- Quantise or shorten only after your eval.
- Count replicas and indexes, not one copy.
- A small recall win can lose on capacity.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A 3072-d model wins 0.4 recall and OOMs pgvector. What do you do? Pick a smaller dim or quantise, re-eval, or move to a store that fits. Do not keep the OOM for a fraction of a point. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Why can ANN quality get worse as dim grows? High-d spaces are harder to index; HNSW/IVF knobs that worked at 384 may need more memory or lose recall at 3072. Measure, do not assume. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: How do you estimate embedding storage? n_vectors × dimensions × bytes per value, plus ANN graph overhead (often multiple times the raw vectors), times replicas. That number gates the model pick. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** When is int8 quantisation acceptable?

When your eval says recall holds (or the loss is worth the RAM) and you have tested the engine's quantised path. Not as a silent default.

**recall.** What do people forget in the spreadsheet?

Graph overhead, replicas, a second index during migration, and the query embedder's RAM if it is local.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Higher dimensions cost RAM and are not automatic quality. I price n × dim × overhead, I quantise only after an eval, and I refuse a 0.5-point win that OOMs the box.

interview.explain:
## What it is

**Interview: why you cannot mix spaces** is one sentence plus a consequence: **different embedders define different geometries; cosine across them is meaningless; a model change is a full re-embed**. You mention the query/doc prefix and the stored model id if they give you time.

This is M4.3's exam. It is short on purpose. Do not wander into training maths.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

It is the most common embedding interview question after 'what is an embedding?'. On the job it is also the incident review when someone upgraded a query model.

## How it works + one small example

Say: 'I pin one model per index. Query and documents use that id. If I change the model I rebuild. Cosine between two models is noise even when the dimensions match.' If they poke: prefixes, two indexes during migration, a guard that refuses a mismatch.

Close: 'Different embedders rotate the space; cosine across models is meaningless.'

## Failure modes

1. **Talking about training** instead of the operational rule.

2. **Saying dim match is enough.**

3. **No re-embed** in the consequence.

4. **Forgetting query vs doc.**


## How you would defend it in a review

Time the sentence. If they cannot say it in fifteen seconds, they do not have the talking point. If they start a paper, stop them and ask for the guard.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- One sentence: different spaces, meaningless cosine, full re-embed.
- Dim match is not compatibility.
- Mention the query/doc guard if they give you time.
- Do not lecture training maths.
- Migration is two indexes, not mixed rows.
- This is the M4.3 talking point.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A candidate explains contrastive loss for three minutes. What did they miss? The operational rule and the incident. Interviewers wanted pin, match, re-embed — not a paper. Then show the change you would ship the same week. They say both models output 768 numbers so it should be fine. Your reply? Dimension is length, not meaning. The axes differ. I would refuse the query or dual-run two indexes, not cosine mixed rows. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Why can you not mix embedding spaces? Give the interview line. Each embedder defines its own geometry. Cosine across models is meaningless, even if dimensions match. Changing a model means re-embedding the corpus and rebuilding the index. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** What operational habit makes this real?

Store model_id on the index and refuse a query embedder that does not match. Without the guard the bug is silent.

**recall.** What one sentence should they remember?

Different embedders rotate the space; cosine across models is meaningless.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Different embedders rotate the space. Cosine across models is meaningless. I pin one model, I match query and docs, and I re-embed when I change it.

cosine-dot-product-euclidean.explain:
## What it is

Three ways to compare vectors. **Cosine similarity** is the cosine of the angle — scale-invariant, the default for many text embedders. **Dot product** (inner product) is cosine if vectors are L2-normalised, otherwise it also rewards magnitude. **Euclidean (L2) distance** is the straight-line distance; smaller is nearer. The **metric must match how the model was trained and how the index is built**. Using L2 on vectors meant for cosine (or the reverse) silently ranks wrong.

Normalise if the vendor says so. pgvector and Qdrant make you pick an operator (`<=>`, cosine, IP, L2). That pick is a contract, not a preference.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask cosine vs L2 vs IP. They want: match the model and the index, cosine is common for text, IP ≡ cosine if normalised. On the job, a wrong operator is a silent quality hole.

## How it works + one small example

Read the model card: 'use cosine' or 'normalise then IP'. Configure the index to that. Example. OpenAI text embeddings: cosine (or IP after norm). A teammate builds L2 on raw vectors; ranking shifts; you rebuild.

Do not compare raw scores across metrics or across models. A 0.2 L2 is not a 0.8 cosine.

## Failure modes

1. **Index L2, query cosine.**

2. **Comparing scores** from two metrics.

3. **Forgetting to normalise** when IP assumes unit vectors.

4. **Picking cosine** because a blog said so, against the card.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask which operator the index uses and why. If they cannot name it, the metric is accidental. Ask what happens if it mismatches the card.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Cosine = angle; IP = cosine if normalised; L2 = distance.
- Metric must match training and the index operator.
- Do not compare scores across metrics or models.
- Normalise when the card says so.
- A wrong operator is a silent recall bug.
- This is a training-and-index decision, not a taste.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. You built an L2 index on a cosine-trained embedder. What do you do? Rebuild with the matching operator (or normalise and use IP if that is the engine's cosine path). Do not tune k on a wrong metric. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Why can you not compare a 0.8 cosine to a 1.2 L2? Different geometries and scales. Thresholds do not transfer. Keep one metric per index. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: When are cosine and inner product the same ranking? When vectors are L2-normalised. Then IP equals cosine up to a constant. If they are not normalised, IP also ranks by magnitude. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Cosine, dot product, and L2 are different geometries. I match the metric to the model and the index. I do not treat a score as portable.

Metric must match training and the index operator.
Do not compare scores across metrics or models.
Normalise when the card says so.
A wrong operator is a silent recall bug.
This is a training-and-index decision, not a taste.
