when-to-skip-transformation.explain:
## What it is

**Skip transformation when baseline retrieval already performs well.** Exact lookups, well-formed FAQs, and a first-stage with high recall do not need a rewrite. Transform is a remedy, not a lifestyle.

This matches 'skip rerank' energy. Defaults stay simple; flags turn extras on per slice.

Skipping is also how you protect identifiers from HyDE drift.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask what you skip in v1. This. On the job, this is the router.

## How it works + one small example

Router: if query looks like an id or recall@k is already high on this class, pass through. Example. 'E-204' → no rewrite. 'why does checkout feel stuck lately' → maybe multi-query.

Re-eval after you improve hybrid; a better baseline retires the rewrite.

## Failure modes

1. **Rewrite always.**

2. **No router.**

3. **HyDE on codes.**

4. **Never re-checking** after retrieve improves.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask the v1 default. If rewrite is always on, push ids. Ask about retiring it after hybrid improves.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Skip when baseline recall is already high.
- Ids and clean FAQs pass through.
- Transform is a remedy, not a default.
- A router (or regex) is enough to start.
- Better retrieve can retire the rewrite.
- HyDE on codes is a skip, not a tune.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Always-on HyDE dropped SKU search quality. Why? Hypothetical docs drifted off the identifier. Skip transform on precise queries; use the raw token in BM25. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you route? A cheap detect (id-like, quoted string, high first-stage score) → pass through. Messy/ambiguous → rewrite or multi-query. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: When do you skip query transformation? When baseline retrieval already performs well: exact ids, clean FAQs, high recall@k. Transform is for the miss class, not every request. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** What happens after you improve hybrid?

Re-eval the rewrite. If baseline now wins, turn the flag off. Do not keep paying for a retired remedy.

**recall.** Is skip the v1 default?

Yes. Ship retrieve-assemble-generate. Add transform when the eval's miss class is 'bad query'.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What to write in the design doc

Copy the key points into the doc as acceptance lines, not as slogans:

- Skip when baseline recall is already high. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Ids and clean FAQs pass through. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Transform is a remedy, not a default. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- A router (or regex) is enough to start. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Better retrieve can retire the rewrite. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- HyDE on codes is a skip, not a tune. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.

A reviewer should be able to tick each line from the PR without asking you to restated the note.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I skip query transformation when baseline retrieve already works — especially exact lookups. Extras are a flag, not the default path.

hyde-failure-on-precise-queries.explain:
## What it is

**HyDE fails on identifier-heavy and precise queries.** The model writes a hypothetical document that is a **plausible essay**, then you retrieve nearest to that essay. An error code, SKU, or API name gets replaced by generic prose; the real runbook never ranks.

HyDE can help **vague conceptual** questions where a fake paragraph sits near real paragraphs. It is the wrong first tool for support tickets.

If you use HyDE, **keep the raw query in BM25** beside it.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is a named failure on the checklist. On the job, it is why HyDE demos look magic and prod SKU search dies.

## How it works + one small example

Ban HyDE when the query matches id-like tokens. Example. 'E-204' → hypothetical 'users see timeouts at checkout…' → dense retrieves essays, misses the E-204 page. BM25 on the raw string would have won.

If you must try HyDE, fuse with the raw-query retrieve so the id can still win.

## Failure modes

1. **HyDE-only** retrieve.

2. **HyDE on SKUs and codes.**

3. **No raw-query channel.**

4. **Treating HyDE as default rewrite.**


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask what HyDE embeds. If they use it on tickets with ids, fail. Hear raw BM25 beside it.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- HyDE embeds a hypothetical doc, not the query.
- Plausible essays miss codes, SKUs, API names.
- Skip HyDE on precise/id queries.
- Keep raw-query BM25 if you try HyDE at all.
- HyDE is for vague conceptual questions, if anything.
- It is not the default rewrite.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. HyDE is on; 'INC-4419' retrieves a similar-incident essay. Fix? Disable HyDE for id-like queries and retrieve the raw string (sparse). Optionally fuse, but never HyDE-only. Then show the change you would ship the same week. When might HyDE help? Vague conceptual questions where a made-up paragraph sits near real explanations and there is no identifier to protect. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Why does HyDE fail on precise queries? It embeds a hypothetical document. On an id or SKU that document becomes generic prose, so dense search misses the exact page. The raw token in BM25 would have hit. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** How do you use HyDE safely if at all?

Fuse HyDE-dense with raw-query BM25 (RRF) and skip HyDE when tokens look like ids.

**recall.** Is HyDE a rewrite?

No. Rewrite keeps a query in query space. HyDE moves to document space. Different drift.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

HyDE drifts off identifiers because it embeds a made-up paragraph. I skip it on precise queries and I keep the raw string in BM25.

It is not the default rewrite.

budget-for-extra-rewrite-calls.explain:
## What it is

**Each transform is another model call; skip on easy lookups.** Budget it like rerank: a cap on extra calls per request, a default-off flag, a slice router. Easy lookups (ids, quoted errors, high first-stage score) pay zero extra.

This is the money twin of 'the extra calls it costs'. Write the budget before you enable the toy.

A daily call cap in settings is a product rule, not only an infra one.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask how you do not go broke. On the job, this is the limiter.

## How it works + one small example

Config: `max_transform_calls=1`, `skip_if_id=true`. Example. 1M easy lookups/day × $0.001 rewrite is a four-figure waste. Route them out.

Alert when average calls/request drift up after a prompt change.

## Failure modes

1. **Unlimited** rewrite fan-out.

2. **No skip_if_id.**

3. **No alert** on calls/request.

4. **Budgeting only generate**, not rewrite.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask for the cap and the skip. If rewrite is unlimited, they have no budget. Ask about ids.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Each transform is a billed call.
- Skip on easy lookups.
- Cap extra calls per request.
- Alert on calls/request drift.
- Budget rewrite, not only the final generate.
- Default off until a slice proves need.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. After a prompt tweak, the bill doubled but answer quality did not. What do you check? Calls/request. A rewrite or multi-query may have started firing on easy lookups. Turn the router back on. Then show the change you would ship the same week. What is a sane v1 cap? Zero extra calls by default; at most one rewrite on the messy slice. Raise N only with a table of recall vs $. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: How do you budget extra rewrite calls? Cap transforms per request, skip easy lookups (ids, high-confidence first-stage), and alert if average calls/request rise. Do not budget only the final generate. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** Why skip ids even if rewrite is 'cheap'?

Cheap × huge QPS is not cheap, and rewrite can drop the id. Two reasons, same skip.

**recall.** What do you alert on?

Average model calls per request and transform-on rate. Quality-only alerts miss the leak.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What to write in the design doc

Copy the key points into the doc as acceptance lines, not as slogans:

- Each transform is a billed call. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Skip on easy lookups. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Cap extra calls per request. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Alert on calls/request drift. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Budget rewrite, not only the final generate. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Default off until a slice proves need. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.

A reviewer should be able to tick each line from the PR without asking you to restated the note.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I budget extra rewrite calls and I skip them on easy lookups. A transform that is always on is a leak, not a feature.

answering-from-evidence.explain:
## What it is

A grounded answer is **generated from retrieved evidence**, not from the model's unsupported memory. The prompt, the schema, and the checker all say: if the span is not in the context, you do not claim it. Style can be parametric; facts cannot.

This is the product promise of RAG. Without it you have a chatbot that sometimes saw a PDF.

Evidence means the **text you assembled**, not 'a document we have somewhere'.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask what grounded means. This. On the job, this is the contract with the user.

## How it works + one small example

Pass only the chunks; forbid outside knowledge; check claims. Example. Context has a 14-day refund; the model knows a 30-day US default — the answer must say 14 and cite, or abstain if the chunk is off-product.

Never add a web-browse silently to 'help'.

## Failure modes

1. **Allowing memory** when sources are thin.

2. **Evidence = 'we have a handbook'** not the assembled text.

3. **No claim check.**

4. **Silent web fallback.**


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask what evidence means. If they say the corpus, not the prompt, they will claim unretrieved pages.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Facts come from assembled chunks, not weights.
- Style may be parametric; claims may not.
- Evidence is the prompt text, not the corpus at large.
- Check claims against that text.
- No silent memory or web fallback.
- This is the user-facing contract.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Context says 14 days; the model answers 30 from training. What failed? Grounding. The generate side used parametric memory. Tighten the prompt/schema and reject unsupported claims. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Is 'we indexed the handbook' enough evidence? No. Evidence is the chunks in this request. An unretrieved page does not support the claim. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What does answering from evidence mean? Every factual claim must be supported by text you put in the prompt. The model's prior knowledge may shape wording, not the fact. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** When may the model use outside knowledge?

For language and structure, or when you explicitly switch out of grounded mode. Not inside a RAG answer path.

**recall.** Why forbid a silent web fallback?

It breaks the contract (uncited, unlogged) and makes retrieve vs generate undebuggable.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I answer from the assembled evidence, not from parametric memory. If the span is not in the prompt, I do not claim it.

Style may be parametric; claims may not.
Evidence is the prompt text, not the corpus at large.
Check claims against that text.
No silent memory or web fallback.
This is the user-facing contract.

attaching-claims-to-sources.explain:
## What it is

**Attach each claim to the chunk that supports it.** Produce **useful citations**: chunk id, quote or offsets, and a user-visible title/link. A blob of footnotes at the end that do not map to sentences is decoration.

Useful means the user can open the span. A PDF filename is a hint, not a source.

Your schema should make the attachment structural (`claims[].citation`) so you can check it.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask how citations work. Per claim. On the job, this is the UI and the checker.

## How it works + one small example

`[{claim, chunk_id, quote}]`. Example. Sentence one → id 17 quote; sentence two → id 4 quote. Render [17] as a link to the section. Drop a sentence whose check fails.

Do not one-cite the whole paragraph if two chunks were used.

## Failure modes

1. **One footnote** for the whole answer.

2. **Titles without spans.**

3. **Citations not aligned** to sentences.

4. **Broken links** to a file the user cannot open.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask to see a claim-to-span map. If citations are a footer list, they are not attached.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Per-claim citations, not one blob.
- Id plus quote (or offsets) plus a usable link.
- Structure it so a checker can run.
- Drop claims that fail the check.
- A filename is not a span.
- Two chunks means two attachments.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. The answer has three facts and one footnote 'handbook.pdf'. What is wrong? No per-claim attachment. You cannot tell which fact is supported or check a span. Split citations by claim. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you store the attachment? In the schema: each claim carries chunk_id and quote. Markdown footnotes are a render, not the source of truth. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What makes a citation useful? It points a claim at a chunk id and a quote or offsets the user can open. A bare filename or a list at the end does not attach the claim. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** What does the UI open?

The section or the quote in the source doc, not a 200-page PDF at page 0.

**recall.** Two chunks support one sentence. What do you attach?

Both ids (or split the sentence). Hiding the second source is how you fail an audit.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

- Structure it so a checker can run. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.

- Two chunks means two attachments. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.

citations-are-not-grounding.explain:
## What it is

**A citation is not grounding.** The cited source must **actually support the claim**. Models will invent a plausible quote, point at a real title, or cite a chunk that is about the same topic but not the fact.

Grounding is a **check**: quote is a substring, and the quote entails the claim (human or judge). Citation is a **pointer**. Pointers can lie.

This is the favourite trap in RAG interviews.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

They will say 'we cite sources' as if that were safety. On the job, this is the audit failure.

## How it works + one small example

Two checks. (1) Quote ∈ chunk. (2) Claim is supported by quote — not merely on-topic. Example. Claim '14-day refund'; cited chunk is a shipping table: on-topic, not supporting. Fail it.

Do not ship a green check for 'has a citation field'.

## Failure modes

1. **Treating presence of a citation as grounded.**

2. **No substring check.**

3. **On-topic chunk** accepted as support.

4. **Invented quotes** that look real.


## How you would defend it in a review

If they equate citations with grounding, fail the point. Ask for the two checks.

## Checks before you merge

abstaining-on-insufficient-evidence.explain:
## What it is

When evidence is **insufficient**, the system **says so** — 'I do not know / not in the docs' — instead of forcing an answer. Insufficient includes empty retrieve, weak scores, failed citation checks, and questions the chunks do not cover.

Abstain is a **first-class output**, not a vibe in the prose. Users trust a bot that can shut up.

A hedge ('it might be 14 or 30') is not abstain; it is a weaker wrong.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask what you do on a miss. Abstain. On the job, this is trust.

## How it works + one small example

Schema path + UI. Example. No chunk survives the checker → `{insufficient_evidence: true, reason: 'no span for refund window'}`. UI shows that, maybe a link to search. Do not emit a number.

Tune how often you abstain on a labelled 'should abstain' set. Too rare is danger; too often is a brick.

## Failure modes

1. **Forced answers** on empty context.

2. **Hedged prose** instead of abstain.

3. **No should-abstain eval.**

4. **Abstain that still includes a guess.**


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask what the user sees on a miss. If a number still appears, it is not abstain.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Insufficient → I do not know, not a guess.
- Empty, weak, failed checks, uncovered questions.
- Abstain is a structured path, not a hedge.
- Eval a should-abstain set.
- A guess inside an abstain is still a guess.
- Users trust a bot that can shut up.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. The bot writes 'it might be 14 days, not sure'. Context is empty. What is wrong? That is a hedge, not abstain, and it still planted a number. Emit the insufficient_evidence path with no fact. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you know you abstain enough? A labelled should-abstain set. Track false answers there and false abstains on answerable items. Tune the gate. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What should RAG do on insufficient evidence? Abstain with a clear I-do-not-know (and why), not a forced or hedged answer. Treat empty retrieve and failed citation checks as insufficient. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** Which events trigger abstain?

Empty retrieve, scores below T, all citations failing the check, or the question not covered by surviving spans.

**recall.** Why not hedge?

Hedges still implant facts and are hard to evaluate. A hard abstain is auditable.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

If the evidence is insufficient I abstain. I do not hedge a number. Abstain is a field and a UI, not a vibe.

keeping-evidence-and-synthesis-distinct.explain:
## What it is

**Keep retrieved evidence and model synthesis distinguishable** in the prompt, the logs, and the UI. Evidence is quoted or boxed with ids. Synthesis is the answer text. If they blur, you cannot check grounding and the user cannot see what was found vs what was written.

In the prompt: a clear `Sources` block vs `Answer`. In the UI: quotes vs the bot's sentence. In the log: two fields.

This is how you debug generate-vs-retrieve and how you pass an audit.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers who have been audited will ask. On the job, this is the screenshot that saves you.

## How it works + one small example

Template and UI. Example. Left: sources with quotes. Right: answer with [ids]. Log `evidence[]` separately from `answer`. Never let the model rewrite the source block.

If you stream, stream the answer; keep sources as structured data.

## Failure modes

1. **One blob** in the log.

2. **Model rewriting** the sources.

3. **UI that only shows the answer.**

4. **Synthesis inside the source block.**


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask to see the UI and the log fields. If sources are invisible, they cannot claim grounding.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Evidence and synthesis are different fields.
- Box and id the sources in the prompt.
- Show sources in the UI, not only the answer.
- Do not let the model rewrite the source block.
- Logs need both, separately.
- Blur kills audits and debugging.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. The model restates a source with a wrong number and the log has one text field. What is lost? You cannot tell original evidence from synthesis. Split the fields; freeze the source block. Then show the change you would ship the same week. What does the UI show besides the answer? The quotes or links for the citations, visually separate from the bot's sentences. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Why keep evidence and synthesis distinct? So you can check grounding, debug retrieve vs generate, and show the user what was found versus what was written. A single blob hides all three. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

**apply.** How do you stop the model rewriting sources?

Put sources in a block the instruction says not to edit, or pass them as a non-rewritable tool result. Check they still match the retrieve log.

**recall.** What two log fields are mandatory?

evidence (ids + text) and answer (plus citations). One concatenated prompt dump is a start, not enough.

quote-then-answer-vs-answer-then-cite.explain:
## What it is

**Quote-then-answer** makes the model **extract supporting spans first**, then write the answer from those spans. **Answer-then-cite** writes the answer first and **invites invented sources** to decorate it. The order is a real generate-side control.

You can enforce quote-first in the schema: `quotes` required before `answer`. Checkers run on the quotes; the answer must stay inside them.

Answer-then-cite can still work if you drop unverified cites — but you will drop a lot.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is a named checklist item. On the job, it is a cheap anti-hallucination.

## How it works + one small example

Schema order: `quotes[]` then `answer` then `insufficient_evidence`. Example. The model must fill quotes first; your code rejects an answer that uses a fact not in quotes.

If the vendor ignores field order, do two calls: extract quotes, then answer — or one structured object you validate regardless of order.

## Failure modes

1. **Answer first**, cites later, no check.

2. **Trusting field order** with no validation.

3. **Quotes that never appear** in the answer path.

4. **Two-call** extract with no budget note.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask which order they use. If answer-then-cite with no drop rule, they will invent sources.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Quote-then-answer reduces invented sources.
- Answer-then-cite invites decoration.
- Require quotes in the schema before you accept an answer.
- Validate support even if field order is ignored.
- Drop unverified cites if you still answer first.
- Two-step extract-then-answer is allowed if you budget it.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. The model answers, then cites a title that was never retrieved. What pattern is that? Answer-then-cite with no check. Require quotes from retrieved ids first, or drop the answer. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you enforce quote-first? A schema that requires quotes[] (with ids) and a checker that the answer stays inside those quotes. Do not rely on the model obeying field order alone. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Why prefer quote-then-answer over answer-then-cite? Writing the answer first invites the model to invent a source that fits the prose. Extracting quotes first constrains the answer to those spans. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** Is answer-then-cite always illegal?

No, if you verify and drop. It is just the pattern that produces more invented sources.

**recall.** What if the API ignores property order?

Validate after the fact, or split into extract then answer. Order in JSON is not a safety boundary.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I extract quotes first and only then answer. Answer-then-cite invites invented sources unless I throw those cites away.

abstain-object-in-the-schema.explain:
## What it is

A required **`insufficient_evidence` path** in the schema **beats a hedged paragraph**. Make it a boolean or an object `{insufficient_evidence: true, reason}` that your parser understands. If the model hedges in `answer` instead, you treat that as a generate failure.

Required means the field exists every time, and your code branches on it before render.

This is structured output applied to grounding.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask how you force abstain. Schema. On the job, this is the branch in the API.

## How it works + one small example

JSON schema: `one of: answer+citations | insufficient_evidence`. Example. Your handler: if insufficient, return 200 with that payload; do not also show `answer`. Unit-test the parser with a hedge-only completion and fail it.

Do not regex 'I do not know' in prose as your only detector.

## Failure modes

1. **Prose-only** abstain.

2. **Answer and abstain both set.**

3. **Optional field** the model skips.

4. **Regex** as the only detector.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask to see the schema. If abstain is prose-only, they will ship hedges. Ask what happens when both fields are set.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Required abstain object > hedged prose.
- Branch on the field before render.
- Do not emit answer and abstain together.
- Unit-test the parser on hedges.
- Regex on prose is a backup, not the path.
- This is structured output for grounding.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. The model sets answer='probably 14 days' and insufficient_evidence=true. What do you render? Abstain only. Dual-filled is a generate failure. Do not show the number. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you test the path? A fixture that must abstain, plus a hedge-only completion that the parser must reject. Do not rely on a live model for the unit test. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Why put abstain in the schema? A required insufficient_evidence path is machine-checkable. A hedged paragraph is easy to miss and hard to evaluate. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** Why not regex I-do-not-know?

Wording varies and a guess can sit next to the phrase. Schema first; regex as telemetry.

**recall.** What does required mean here?

The object always chooses a path (answer+cites or abstain). A missing field is a parse error, not a silent answer.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I put insufficient_evidence in the schema as a required path. A hedged paragraph is not an abstain I can ship.

naive-advanced-adaptive-rag.explain:
## What it is

A map, not a ladder you must climb. **Naive RAG**: retrieve once, generate. **Advanced RAG**: better chunking, hybrid, rerank, rewrite — still mostly one shot. **Adaptive / self-correcting RAG**: the system **decides** whether to retrieve, whether to retry, and whether the evidence is good enough.

Do not treat later names as strictly better. Each step adds ops and failure modes. You move when a **named failure** on the baseline demands it.

This module is a catalogue. The last notes tell you how to pick.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask naive vs advanced vs adaptive. Three boxes. On the job, this is the vocabulary.

## How it works + one small example

Place your system. Example. M4.9 baseline = naive (or lightly advanced if hybrid). Add rerank/rewrite = advanced. Add a grader that re-retrieves = adaptive.

Say which failure moved you. 'We read a paper' is not a move.

## Failure modes

1. **Skipping naive** to start at adaptive.

2. **Calling any rerank** Self-RAG.

3. **Assuming more advanced is better.**

4. **No named failure** for the jump.


## How you would defend it in a review

Hear three boxes and a named-failure rule. If they skip to Self-RAG, pull them back.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Naive = one retrieve, generate.
- Advanced = hybrid, rerank, rewrite, still mostly one shot.
- Adaptive = decide, retry, grade evidence.
- Later is not automatically better.
- Move on a named failure.
- This is a map, not a prestige ladder.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A team starts with Self-RAG and has no baseline numbers. What is wrong? They skipped naive/advanced measurement. You cannot know adaptive helped. Build the baseline first. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Where does hybrid+rerank sit? Advanced. It is still one retrieve path, just a better one. Adaptive would add a decide/retry loop. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Contrast naive, advanced, and adaptive RAG. Naive retrieves once and generates. Advanced improves that retrieve (chunk, hybrid, rerank, rewrite) but is still mostly one pass. Adaptive decides whether to retrieve, which strategy, and whether to correct after a grade. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** What justifies leaving naive?

A measured miss: low recall, id queries, drowning k. Not a blog title.

**recall.** Is adaptive always the goal?

No. It adds calls and new failure modes. Stay advanced if the judge is already happy.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Naive is retrieve-once; advanced adds retrieve quality tricks; adaptive decides and corrects. I climb only for a named failure, not for a paper.

Advanced = hybrid, rerank, rewrite, still mostly one shot.
Adaptive = decide, retry, grade evidence.
Later is not automatically better.
Move on a named failure.
This is a map, not a prestige ladder.

questions.q: A team starts with Self-RAG and has no baseline numbers. What is wrong?
questions.a: They skipped naive/advanced measurement. You cannot know adaptive helped. Build the baseline first.

questions.q: Where does hybrid+rerank sit?
questions.a: Advanced. It is still one retrieve path, just a better one. Adaptive would add a decide/retry loop.

questions.q: What justifies leaving naive?
questions.a: A measured miss: low recall, id queries, drowning k. Not a blog title.

questions.q: Is adaptive always the goal?
questions.a: No. It adds calls and new failure modes. Stay advanced if the judge is already happy.

self-rag.explain:
## What it is

**Self-RAG**: the model **retrieves when needed** and **reflects** on the evidence and its own draft (special tokens or a grader: retrieve? relevant? supported?). It is adaptive on the generate side: not every question hits the index, and a bad span can trigger another look.

You can approximate it without the original tokens: a small router + a support check + an optional second retrieve.

It is not 'the model is sentient'. It is extra decisions with extra calls.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

They will name Self-RAG. On the job, steal the decisions, not the paper's token set.

## How it works + one small example

Decisions: need retrieve? evidence ok? answer supported? Example. 'hello' → no retrieve. Policy question → retrieve. Unsupported draft → retrieve again or abstain.

Implement as explicit steps you can log, not a mystery decode.

## Failure modes

1. **Self-RAG as a vibe** with no decisions logged.

2. **Retrieving always** and still calling it Self-RAG.

3. **No support check.**

4. **Copying tokens** you cannot run.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask which decisions they log. If they only say the paper name, they do not have Self-RAG.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Retrieve-when-needed plus reflection on evidence and draft.
- Approximate with a router and a support check.
- Always-retrieve is not Self-RAG.
- Log each decision.
- Extra calls are the price.
- Steal the decisions, not the token scheme.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A pipeline always retrieves and never checks support. Is it Self-RAG? No. The name requires the decisions. You built naive or advanced RAG with extra branding. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you approximate it in production? A cheap router (retrieve?), a relevance/support grader, and a retry or abstain. Log each bit. Skip the original special tokens if you do not have that model. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What does Self-RAG add over naive RAG? A decision to retrieve or not, and reflection on whether evidence is relevant and whether the draft is supported — with a possible retry or abstain. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** When is the retrieve-when-needed part enough alone?

When many questions are chitchat or closed-book. You still need a support check for the ones that do retrieve.

**recall.** What do you tell a PM who wants Self-RAG on the slide?

Name the decisions and the extra calls. The paper name is not a feature.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Self-RAG retrieves when needed and reflects on evidence and the draft. I implement those decisions as logged steps, not as magic tokens.

Approximate with a router and a support check.

crag-corrective-rag.explain:
## What it is

**CRAG (Corrective RAG)** **evaluates retrieved evidence** and **triggers corrective retrieval** (or web, or another query) when the first set is weak. The new idea is a **grader on the first retrieve**, not a fancier first retrieve.

If the grader says the chunks are irrelevant, you do not generate from them. You correct or abstain.

It is a named fix for **bad first retrieval**, which is why the later 'pick from the failure' note points here.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will contrast CRAG and Self-RAG. On the job, this is a retry loop with a gate.

## How it works + one small example

`chunks = retrieve(q)`; `ok = grade(q, chunks)`; if not ok: `chunks = retrieve(rewrite(q))` or abstain. Example. First retrieve is off-topic; grader says no; second query is decontextualised; then generate or abstain.

Cap retries at 1. Infinite correct is a loop incident.

## Failure modes

1. **No cap** on corrective hops.

2. **Generating from chunks the grader rejected.**

3. **No grader**, just always retrieve twice.

4. **Web correct** without a policy.


## How you would defend it in a review

Hear a grader and a cap. If they always retrieve twice, it is not CRAG. Ask what happens to rejected chunks.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- CRAG = grade first retrieve, then correct or abstain.
- It targets bad first retrieval.
- Do not generate from rejected chunks.
- Cap corrective hops (usually 1).
- Always-twice is not CRAG.
- Web correction needs a product policy.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. The grader says irrelevant but you still send those chunks. What did you build? A log line, not CRAG. Corrective means you do not generate from the rejected set. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How does CRAG differ from Self-RAG in one line? CRAG focuses on correcting a weak retrieve. Self-RAG also decides whether to retrieve and whether the draft is supported. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What does Corrective RAG do? It evaluates the first retrieved set and, if weak, triggers another retrieve (or a fallback) instead of generating from bad evidence. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** Why cap retries?

A loop of rewrite+retrieve will blow p95 and $ and can oscillate. One correction then abstain is enough for v1.

**recall.** Is always retrieving twice CRAG?

No. The grade is the point. Always-twice is just 2× latency.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

CRAG grades the first retrieve and corrects or abstains when it is weak. I cap retries and I do not generate from rejected chunks.

It targets bad first retrieval.
Do not generate from rejected chunks.
Cap corrective hops (usually 1).
Always-twice is not CRAG.
Web correction needs a product policy.

adaptive-rag.explain:
## What it is

**Adaptive RAG** **dynamically chooses** whether retrieval is required and **which strategy** (BM25, dense, hybrid, multi-query, none). A router sits in front: chitchat → no retrieve; id → sparse; messy → hybrid+rewrite.

It is the strategy layer, not a new index. You can implement it with rules before you train a classifier.

Adaptive without logs is just a pile of ifs you cannot tune.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

They will say adaptive. On the job, this is the router you already wanted in M4.11.

## How it works + one small example

Start with rules: id-like → BM25; short greeting → no retrieve; else hybrid. Example. Graduate to a small classifier when the rule file is a novel.

Log the route name on every request. Eval per route.

## Failure modes

1. **One path** and calling it adaptive.

2. **No route log.**

3. **A 20-branch router** with no eval.

4. **Retrieving always** 'just in case'.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask how they choose a strategy. If there is one path, it is not adaptive. Ask for the route log.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Adaptive = whether to retrieve + which strategy.
- Rules first, classifier later.
- Log the route name.
- Eval per route, not one global score.
- One path is not adaptive.
- Just-in-case retrieve is the opposite.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Every request hits hybrid+HyDE+rerank. Adaptive? No. That is a single expensive path. Adaptive would skip most of that on easy lookups. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you start without a trained router? Rules on the query (id-like, greeting, length, '? and') mapped to strategies. Log and replace rules that fire wrongly. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What does Adaptive RAG choose? Whether retrieval is needed and which retrieval strategy to run (sparse, dense, hybrid, multi-query, none). Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** What do you eval?

Quality, latency, and $ per route. A global score hides a broken id path.

**recall.** Why log the route?

So you can see that 80% of QPS did not need HyDE, and so an incident has a name.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What to write in the design doc

Copy the key points into the doc as acceptance lines, not as slogans:

- Adaptive = whether to retrieve + which strategy. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Rules first, classifier later. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Log the route name. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Eval per route, not one global score. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- One path is not adaptive. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Just-in-case retrieve is the opposite. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.

A reviewer should be able to tick each line from the PR without asking you to restated the note.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Adaptive RAG picks whether to retrieve and which strategy. I start with rules, I log the route, and I do not retrieve just in case.

iterative-rag.explain:
## What it is

**Iterative RAG** repeats **retrieve and generate until enough evidence** (or a cap). The draft or missing slots become the next query. It is for **gaps**, not for style.

Without a stop condition you have a loop. Stop: enough slots filled, grader says supported, or N=2.

This overlaps CRAG (correct) and multi-hop (chain). Iterative is the generic loop.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

They will say iterative. On the job, this is a loop with a budget.

## How it works + one small example

`for i in 1..N: retrieve; grade; if ok: generate; break; else: new_query`. Example. First answer missing the date; second query asks for the date span; then final generate.

Do not iterate on greetings.

## Failure modes

1. **No N cap.**

2. **Iterating when the first retrieve was fine.**

3. **Using the full draft** as the next query (noise).

4. **No stop on supported.**


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask for N and the stop. If they iterate without a cap, fail. Ask what the next query is.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Loop retrieve/generate until enough or N.
- Stop on supported, filled slots, or cap.
- For gaps, not style.
- Do not iterate easy lookups.
- Next query is a slot, not the whole draft.
- Overlaps CRAG and multi-hop; this is the generic loop.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A loop ran 8 times on 'hello'. What is missing? A router and a cap. Greetings should not enter the loop. N should be 1–2. Then show the change you would ship the same week. What should the next query be? The missing slot or a rewrite of the weak part — not the entire previous essay. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What is iterative RAG? Retrieve and generate repeat until evidence is sufficient or a cap is hit. The next query is driven by missing slots or a failed grade. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** How does it relate to CRAG?

CRAG is a named one-correction pattern. Iterative is the generic loop that can include that correction.

**recall.** What are the stop conditions?

Grader says supported, required slots filled, or N reached (then abstain or answer with what you have, per policy).

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What to write in the design doc

Copy the key points into the doc as acceptance lines, not as slogans:

- Loop retrieve/generate until enough or N. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Stop on supported, filled slots, or cap. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- For gaps, not style. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Do not iterate easy lookups. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Next query is a slot, not the whole draft. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Overlaps CRAG and multi-hop; this is the generic loop. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.

A reviewer should be able to tick each line from the PR without asking you to restated the note.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Iterative RAG loops retrieve and generate until evidence is enough or the cap hits. I always have N and a supported-stop.

multi-hop-rag.explain:
## What it is

**Multi-hop RAG** needs **several retrieval steps** or **combining evidence from multiple sources** because the answer is a **chain** (A leads to B). One query cannot hold the chain. Example: who owns the service that pages on E-204? First hop finds E-204's service; second finds the owner.

It is not 'we retrieve 50'. It is **sequential dependence**. Parallel multi-query is not multi-hop unless hop 2 uses hop 1.

This is the failure mode the later pick-note assigns to multi-hop.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will give a chain question. On the job, this is why one-shot RAG looks dumb on org charts.

## How it works + one small example

Plan hops or extract the next entity. Example. Hop 1: E-204 → service checkout-api. Hop 2: checkout-api owner → team X. Then generate from both.

Cap hops. Persist intermediate entities in the log.

## Failure modes

1. **Calling top-k=50** multi-hop.

2. **No intermediate entity** stored.

3. **Unbounded hops.**

4. **Parallel queries** labelled multi-hop.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask for a chain example. If they say 'we retrieve more', it is not multi-hop. Hear hop 2 depending on hop 1.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Multi-hop = sequential, dependent retrieves.
- Bigger k is not multi-hop.
- Parallel multi-query is not multi-hop.
- Store intermediate entities.
- Cap hops; then abstain.
- For chained facts (the pick-note).

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. You raised k to 50 so both hops sit in the window. Is that multi-hop? No. That is hoping a chain fits. Real multi-hop queries the second entity after the first retrieve. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Give a hop plan for 'who owns the service that throws E-204'. Hop 1: E-204 → service name. Hop 2: that service → owner team. Then generate from both spans. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What makes retrieval multi-hop? A later retrieve depends on an entity or fact from an earlier one. Combining two independent lists is not enough. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** What do you log between hops?

The extracted entity and the chunk it came from. Otherwise hop 2 is un-auditable.

**recall.** How is this different from RAG-Fusion?

Fusion runs independent queries in parallel and merges ranks. Multi-hop is sequential and dependent.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Multi-hop is a chain: hop 2 needs hop 1's entity. I do not call a bigger k multi-hop, and I cap the hops.

Bigger k is not multi-hop.
Parallel multi-query is not multi-hop.
Store intermediate entities.

For chained facts (the pick-note).

graph-rag.explain:
## What it is

**Graph RAG** stores **entities and relations** (and often community summaries) and retrieves along the **graph**, not only by vector similarity. Useful when the question is about **connections** or a **global** theme spread across many docs.

It is another index you must **build and maintain**. It is not a free upgrade to naive RAG.

You still may use vectors to find a start node. The graph is the structure on top.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

They will say Graph RAG as if it were default 2026. On the job, the next notes are the cold water.

## How it works + one small example

Extract entities/edges at ingest; query by expanding neighbours or by community summaries for global questions. Example. 'How do billing and checkout fail together?' needs edges, not the nearest FAQ.

Do not start here (ops-cost note).

## Failure modes

1. **Graph as v1.**

2. **Stale edges** after a doc update.

3. **No eval** vs vector baseline.

4. **Calling a knowledge graph** Graph RAG with no retrieve path.


## How you would defend it in a review

Hear entities plus a retrieve path. If they start v1 here, push to the ops-cost note. Ask about stale edges.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Graph = entities, relations, maybe community summaries.
- For connections and global questions.
- Another index to maintain.
- Vectors may still find the start node.
- Not v1.
- A graph without a retrieve path is not Graph RAG.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Docs updated; answers still mention a retired service. What drifted? The graph. Edges and community summaries need the same incremental ingest as chunks. A stale graph is a stale index. Then show the change you would ship the same week. When is a vector store enough instead? Local factoid questions a chunk can answer. Graphs earn their keep on relations and global themes. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What does Graph RAG retrieve over? A graph of entities and relationships (and often summaries of communities), not only nearest vectors. Vector search may still seed the start nodes. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** What must ingest do extra?

Entity/relation extraction (and maybe clustering/summaries), versioned with the chunks so deletes tombstone edges too.

**recall.** Is a knowledge graph automatically Graph RAG?

No. You still need a retrieve-and-generate path that uses the graph. A triple store alone is not RAG.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Graph RAG retrieves on entities and relations, not only cosine. I use it for connected or global questions, and I do not start there.

when-graph-rag-is-useful.explain:
## What it is

Graph RAG earns its keep on **highly connected knowledge**, **entity relationships**, **global questions**, and **facts spread across many documents**. Org charts, dependency maps, 'themes this quarter', 'who is affected if X dies'.

It does **not** earn its keep on 'what is the refund window' — a chunk will do. Use the graph when **cosine cannot see the path**.

If you cannot name the relation, you do not need the graph.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will ask when. Four jobs. On the job, this is the go/no-go.

## How it works + one small example

Name the question type. Example. 'Summarise how on-call owns checkout' → relations. 'What does error E-204 mean' → a chunk. 'What themes appear across 400 postmortems' → community summaries.

Prototype the question on naive RAG. If hops fail, consider the graph.

## Failure modes

1. **Graph for factoids.**

2. **No named relation.**

3. **Global-summary questions** answered with top-5 chunks (lossy) without considering a graph or map-reduce.

4. **Graph because a vendor demoed it.**


## How you would defend it in a review

Hear a relation-shaped question. If they graph a FAQ, push. Ask what they tried first.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Useful: connections, relations, global, spread-out facts.
- Not useful: local factoids a chunk answers.
- If you cannot name the relation, skip the graph.
- Prototype the question on naive RAG first.
- Vendor demos are not a question type.
- Cosine cannot see a multi-edge path.

## What it is

Two crisp maps. **Multi-hop for chained facts. Corrective RAG for bad first retrieval.** Add: hybrid for ids+paraphrase; rewrite for poor queries; rerank for disorder in a good shortlist; graph for relations/global; adaptive router when the mix is wide.

Memorise the two on the checklist; the rest you can derive.

Picking from the failure is how you avoid the catalogue becoming a shopping list.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is a named talking point. On the job, it is the decision tree on the wiki.

## How it works + one small example

One sentence per miss. Example. Gold never in top-50 → retrieve/hybrid/chunk, not Self-RAG. Gold in 50 but not in 4 → rerank. First retrieve off-topic → CRAG. Need entity from hop 1 → multi-hop.

Write this as a runbook, not a slide of logos.

## Failure modes

1. **One favourite variant** for every miss.

2. **Self-RAG for a chunking bug.**

3. **Graph for an id miss.**

4. **No runbook.**


## How you would defend it in a review

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Multi-hop → chained facts.
- CRAG → bad first retrieval.
- Hybrid → ids plus paraphrase.
- Rewrite → poor queries; rerank → disorder in the shortlist.
- Graph → relations/global.

graph-rag-ops-cost.explain:
## What it is

**Entity graphs need maintenance; do not start there.** You pay extraction (LLM or NER) on every ingest, versioning of edges, stale-node cleanup, community re-summaries, and a second query path. That is real ops, not a library import.

Start with naive/advanced RAG. Graduate to a graph when a **named relation question** fails and a hop plan is not enough.

A weekend graph on a demo corpus is not a production graph.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the last checklist item and the cold water. On the job, it is the staffing conversation.

## How it works + one small example

List the jobs: extract, resolve entities, apply deletes, rebuild summaries, eval vs chunk baseline, page someone when extraction drifts. Example. 10k docs × extract on every update is a bill and a queue.

If you cannot staff that, you cannot staff Graph RAG.

## Failure modes

1. **Starting at the graph.**

2. **No delete path** for edges.

3. **Never rebuilding** summaries.

4. **Demo corpus** as proof of ops.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask who owns extract and deletes. If nobody, they cannot start at a graph. Hear the hop-plan alternative.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Graphs add extract, resolve, delete, re-summarise.
- Do not start there.
- A hop plan is cheaper to try first.
- Deletes must tombstone edges.
- Demo ops are not prod ops.
- If you cannot staff ingest, you cannot staff the graph.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A team ships Graph RAG in week one of a new corpus. What do you change? Start with chunk RAG. Try multi-hop if needed. Add a graph when a named relation question still fails and someone owns ingest. Then show the change you would ship the same week. What happens on a doc delete? Tombstone chunks and their edges (and maybe refresh community summaries). A leftover edge is a stale fact. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: Why is Graph RAG expensive to operate? Every ingest must extract and resolve entities, apply deletes to edges, and often rebuild summaries. That is a second pipeline besides chunks. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** What must you staff?

The extract/resolve path, drift eval, and on-call for the graph query path — not only the chat API.

**recall.** What one line should they remember?

Entity graphs need maintenance; do not start there.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Graphs need extraction, versioning, and deletes. I do not start there. I graduate only when a relation question beats a hop plan and we can staff the ingest.

## What it is

**Rebuild the hand-built pipeline** in **LlamaIndex or LangChain** (or both, once). Same ingest, chunk, retrieve, assemble, generate, cite, abstain — but using their indexes and query engines. The point is **parity**, not a new product.

You already know the verbs (M4.9). The framework is a faster way to wire them, and a new way to hide them.

Do this after the baseline works. Framework-first is how you skip M4.9.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

It is the capstone. On the job, this is how you evaluate a library.

## How it works + one small example

Pick one framework. Map each verb to an object (index, retriever, synthesizer / query engine). Example. Same two-doc fixture as M4.9 must still abstain and cite.

Keep your prompt visible (next notes). Do not enable every integration.

## Failure modes

1. **Framework without a baseline.**

2. **Different chunking** so parity is meaningless.

3. **Enabling every extra** on day one.

4. **Cannot find the prompt.**


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask which verbs map to which objects. If there is no baseline fixture, they rebuilt nothing.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Rebuild, do not replace, the hand-built verbs.
- Same fixture: cite and abstain must still hold.
- After M4.9, not instead of it.
- Map each verb to one object you can name.
- Do not enable every extra on day one.
- Pick one framework first.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A teammate starts the level in LlamaIndex with no baseline. What is the risk? They cannot print or parity-test the prompt. Hidden defaults will own grounding. Do M4.9 first. Then show the change you would ship the same week. What must the two-doc fixture still do? Answer from A, answer from B, abstain on neither, with checkable citations. If the framework loses that, you are not done. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What are you rebuilding in a framework? The hand-built pipeline: ingest, chunk, retrieve, assemble, generate, cite, abstain — with the same fixture. Not a new app. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. **apply.** Why one framework first?

So you learn the map. Two at once is a compare before you can see either prompt.

**recall.** Is a different chunker allowed in the rebuild?

Not for the first parity test. Change one variable after the baseline matches.

indexes-retrievers-query-engines.explain:
## What it is

Framework vocabulary. **Index**: stored vectors/text (and how they were built). **Retriever**: the object that returns nodes for a query (vector, BM25, hybrid, router). **Query engine**: retrieve + synthesize (assemble+generate). Citations and node metadata ride along if you configured them.

You should be able to **swap the retriever** without rewriting the engine, and to **call the retriever alone** in a test.

If you only ever call `query()`, you cannot debug.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interviewers will use these words. On the job, this is how you navigate the docs.

## How it works + one small example

Print types. Example. `index.as_retriever(k=10)` then your own assemble; or `as_query_engine` for the full path. Unit-test the retriever with the two-doc fixture (ids only).

Read the constructor kwargs: embed model, chunker, similarity top k.

## Failure modes

1. **Only query()** in production.

2. **Cannot list nodes** without generating.

3. **Unknown embed model** on the index.

4. **Mixing two indexes'** retrievers blindly.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask them to get nodes without generating. If they cannot, they only have query(). Ask which embedder the index uses.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Index = stored data + build choices.
- Retriever = nodes for a query.
- Query engine = retrieve + synthesize.
- Call the retriever alone in tests.
- Know the embedder and k on the index.
- query() only is undebuggable.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. You can only call query() and cannot print nodes. What do you add? A retriever handle (as_retriever / getRelevantDocuments) and a log of node ids before synthesize. Then show the change you would ship the same week. Why swap retrievers under one engine? To A/B hybrid vs vector without rewriting assemble. That is the point of the split. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What do index, retriever, and query engine mean in LlamaIndex/LangChain? The index is the stored corpus and build. The retriever returns nodes for a query. The query engine retrieves and synthesizes an answer. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** What constructor facts must you record?

Embed model id, chunker, k, metric. They are the same contracts as the hand-built path.

**recall.** Can you unit-test a query engine like a retriever?

You can, but you will mock the LLM. Test the retriever with no LLM first — it is cheaper and catches id bugs.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Index stores, retriever proposes nodes, query engine synthesizes. I can call the retriever alone and I know which embedder the index used.

framework-reranking-query-transforms.explain:
## What it is

Frameworks ship **rerankers and query transforms** as components (postprocessors, compressors, rewrite chains). Use them to rebuild **the same extras** you would have wired by hand — not a junk drawer of every class in the docs.

Wire one extra at a time, behind a flag, with the same eval as M4.10–M4.11.

A component you cannot log is worse than hand-rolled.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

The checklist asks you to implement common improvements via the framework. On the job, this is copy-paste temptation.

## How it works + one small example

Add a reranker postprocessor; log the reorder. Or a rewrite chain; log the rewritten query. Example. Same 50→8→4 shape. Do not also enable a compressor, a HyDE transform, and a router on the same afternoon.

Parity: extras must not drop abstain.

## Failure modes

1. **Every postprocessor** enabled.

2. **No log** of rewrite or rerank.

3. **Losing abstain** after a component.

4. **Different k** than the hand-built extra.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask how many extras are on. If more than one unmeasured, push. Ask whether abstain still fires.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Rerank and rewrite exist as framework components.
- One extra at a time, flagged.
- Log rewrite text and rerank order.
- Abstain must survive the component.
- Same 50→8→4 (or your numbers) as hand-built.
- Junk-drawer enable is not an implementation.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. Enabling a compressor dropped citations. What do you do? Turn it off, then see what it removed from the nodes. A component that eats spans is not an improvement. Then show the change you would ship the same week. What do you log for a rewrite chain? The rewritten query (or queries) and which transform ran — same as M4.11. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: How should you add rerank or query transform in a framework? As one component at a time, logged, evaluated the same way as the hand-built version, without turning on every extra in the docs. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** What shape should a framework reranker keep?

Shortlist in, fewer nodes out (e.g. 50→8). If it reranks the corpus, you miswired it.

**recall.** Why match the hand-built extra?

So parity tells you the framework did not change behaviour. Two different designs cannot be compared.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I add framework rerankers and transforms one at a time, with logs and the same eval as the hand-built extras. I do not enable the junk drawer.

framework-vs-hand-built.explain:
## What it is

Compare on **control, development speed, debugging, and complexity**. Frameworks win **speed** (indexes, loaders, components). Hand-built wins **control and debugging** (you can print the prompt). Complexity can go either way: a thin framework use is fine; a deep graph of runnables is not.

The honest answer in an interview is **both**: baseline by hand, extras maybe in a framework you can still inspect.

There is no moral victory for either camp.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

They will ask which is better. Trade table. On the job, this is the team argument.

## How it works + one small example

Four columns. Example. Speed: framework. Control: hand. Debug: hand unless you logged every component. Complexity: framework can hide or explode.

Pick per surface: ingest loaders maybe framework; assemble prompt maybe hand.

## Failure modes

1. **Always framework.**

2. **Always hand** as purity.

3. **No debug story** for the framework path.

4. **Complexity** ignored.


## How you would defend it in a review

Hear the four columns. If they pick a camp with no debug story, push. Mixing is allowed.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Columns: control, speed, debug, complexity.
- Framework → speed; hand → control/debug.
- Complexity can explode in either direction.
- Both: hand baseline, inspectable framework extras.
- No moral victory.
- Mix per surface if that keeps the prompt visible.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A team cannot print the assembled context in LangChain. Who is winning? Nobody. Speed without debug is a trap. Add callbacks/logging or pull assemble back in-house. Then show the change you would ship the same week. When is the framework the right default? When loaders/indexes would take a week by hand and you have already proven the prompt and abstain on a baseline. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: How do you compare a framework RAG to the hand-built one? On control, development speed, debugging, and complexity — not on brand. Frameworks usually win speed; hand-built usually wins inspectability. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** When do you stay hand-built?

When the prompt is the product (grounding, citations) and the framework hides it, or when the graph of runnables is harder than 200 lines.

**recall.** Is mixing allowed?

Yes: framework retriever, hand assemble. The split is the point of the vocabulary.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Frameworks buy speed; hand-built buys control and debugging. I use a framework where I can still inspect retrieve and generate, and I keep the baseline by hand.

Complexity can explode in either direction.
Both: hand baseline, inspectable framework extras.
No moral victory.
Mix per surface if that keeps the prompt visible.
