frameworks-hide-the-prompt.explain:
## What it is

**Log the final assembled context before you trust the abstraction.** Frameworks stitch system prompts, node templates, and output parsers you did not write. If you cannot print the exact messages, you cannot split retrieve vs generate or check grounding.

Callbacks, verbose flags, or a custom synthesizer that you own are the fix — not hope.

This is the most important M4.14 operational note.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Every framework incident starts here. Interviewers who have been burned will ask.

## How it works + one small example

On every request (or sampled): dump messages/token counts/node ids. Example. You discover a default 'use your knowledge if needed' line. Delete it.

Add a test that the dump does not contain that line and does contain your abstain rule.

## Failure modes

1. **No dump.**

2. **Trusting default prompts.**

3. **A verbose flag only on localhost.**

4. **Token count unknown.**


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask to see a dumped prompt from prod. If they have never printed it, they do not trust the stack — they hope.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Print the final messages; do not trust defaults.
- Defaults may invite outside knowledge.
- Callbacks or a custom synthesizer you own.
- Test that abstain wording is present.
- Do this in prod samples, not only localhost.
- No dump, no grounding claim.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. The model uses outside knowledge; your code never said it could. Where do you look? The hidden default prompt. Dump it. Frameworks often include a helpful-assistant line that undoes your rule. Then show the change you would ship the same week. How do you keep the dump honest in prod? Sampled logging of messages (redact if needed) plus a test that the abstain rule is in the template. Localhost verbose is not enough. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What must you log when a framework assembles the prompt? The final messages (or equivalent), node ids, and token counts. Without that you cannot debug or claim grounding. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** What if the framework will not give you the messages?

Custom synthesizer or leave assemble hand-built. An opaque generate is a no-go for this product.

**recall.** What one line should they remember?

Log the final assembled context before you trust the abstraction.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Frameworks hide the prompt. I log the final assembled messages before I trust the stack, and I test that my abstain rule is actually in there.

Callbacks or a custom synthesizer you own.
Test that abstain wording is present.

No dump, no grounding claim.

parity-test-vs-the-hand-built-baseline.explain:
## What it is

A framework **must not lose the abstain or citation rule**. The **parity test** is the same fixture and the same judge: answers still cite quote-plus-id, still abstain on the uncovered question, still do not cite unretrieved titles.

If parity fails, the framework is not done — no matter how fast the demo looks.

Run parity on every framework upgrade.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the acceptance test for M4.14. On the job, this is the regression gate.

## How it works + one small example

Same three questions as M4.9. Example. Framework answers the uncovered one: fail. Citations become titles-only: fail. Then add a gold-span check.

Automate it. A notebook compare is a start; a CI test is the finish.

## Failure modes

1. **No shared fixture.**

2. **Shipping after a prettier demo** that lost abstain.

3. **Parity only once.**

4. **Different questions** so of course they differ.


## How you would defend it in a review

Ask to see the CI fixture. If parity was a demo afternoon, it will rot on the next upgrade.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Same fixture, same judge, same rules.
- Abstain and quote-plus-id must survive.
- No unretrieved titles.
- Parity on every upgrade.
- A prettier demo that fails parity is a fail.
- Automate it.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. The framework demo looks better but answers the uncovered question. Ship? No. It lost abstain. Fix the prompt/engine or keep the hand-built generate path. Then show the change you would ship the same week. When do you re-run parity? On every framework or prompt-template upgrade, and when you add a component. Once is not a gate. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: What is the parity test against the hand-built baseline? The same fixture and judge: still cite quote-plus-id, still abstain on uncovered questions, still never cite an unretrieved title. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** Why the same questions?

Otherwise you are comparing two products. Parity is a regression, not a vibe.

**recall.** What one line should they remember?

A framework must not lose the abstain or citation rule.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What to write in the design doc

Copy the key points into the doc as acceptance lines, not as slogans:

- Same fixture, same judge, same rules. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Abstain and quote-plus-id must survive. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- No unretrieved titles. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Parity on every upgrade. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- A prettier demo that fails parity is a fail. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Automate it. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.

A reviewer should be able to tick each line from the PR without asking you to restated the note.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The framework must pass the same abstain and citation fixture as the hand-built baseline. If it loses those, it is not a rebuild.

interview.explain:
## What it is

**Interview: defend a framework choice** — **speed of iteration, then show you can still inspect retrieve and generate.** Name the trade (M4.14's compare note) and the dump. If you cannot inspect, you do not get to claim the framework.

They want an adult, not a fan.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

It is the capstone talking point. On the job, it is also how you say no to an opaque stack.

## How it works + one small example

Say: 'I used LlamaIndex (or LangChain) to move faster on loaders and indexes after a hand-built baseline. I can print node ids and the final messages. Parity still abstains. If I could not inspect, I would keep assemble in-house.'

If they poke lock-in: thin wrappers, retriever interface.

## Failure modes

1. **Brand loyalty** with no inspect story.

2. **Purity** with no speed story.

3. **No baseline** in the pitch.

4. **No parity.**


## How you would defend it in a review

Hear speed plus a dump. If they only name a brand, fail the talking point. Ask about the baseline.

## Checks before you merge

Treat each line as something a reviewer can point at in the diff, a test, or a log field:

- Speed first, then inspectability.
- Hand-built baseline is in the pitch.
- Dump nodes and messages or do not claim the framework.
- Parity on abstain and citations.
- Thin wrappers beat lock-in fear.
- Adult, not fan.

If a line is only a slogan, the note is not implemented. Add the artefact in the same PR as the feature.

## If they say this is over-engineering

Walk the failure first. A candidate says 'LangChain is industry standard'. What is missing? Inspectability, parity, and a reason the baseline was not enough. Industry is not a defence. Then show the change you would ship the same week. What do you show on the laptop? A dumped prompt and a retriever-only call that returns the two fixture ids. Not a logo. That pair is why the extra lines exist: one prevents an incident, the other is small enough to merge.

## Fifteen-minute lab

Recite the recall answer cold: How do you defend a framework choice in an interview? Speed of iteration after a hand-built baseline, plus proof you can inspect retrieve (node ids) and generate (final messages), plus parity on abstain and citations. Then reproduce the happy path once, inject the debug failure on purpose, and confirm the log or the user-visible state matches this note. If you cannot break it deliberately, you cannot claim you handle it. Keep the lab on a fake model or a fixture so it runs without a bill.

## Drill the rest of the questions

These are the remaining questions from this note. Answer out loud, then read the model line and mark what you skipped:

**apply.** What if inspectability is missing?

You do not defend the framework — you unwrap assemble or switch. Speed without eyes is not a defence.

**recall.** What one line should they remember?

Speed of iteration, then show you can still inspect retrieve and generate.

If a line surprised you, that gap is the next lab — not a new paper.

## What to write in the design doc

Copy the key points into the doc as acceptance lines, not as slogans:

- Speed first, then inspectability. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Hand-built baseline is in the pitch. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Dump nodes and messages or do not claim the framework. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Parity on abstain and citations. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Thin wrappers beat lock-in fear. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.
- Adult, not fan. — write the log field, test, or user-visible string that proves it.

A reviewer should be able to tick each line from the PR without asking you to restated the note.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I pick a framework for speed of iteration after a hand-built baseline, and I defend it by showing I can still inspect retrieve and generate.

Dump nodes and messages or do not claim the framework.
